en: Preface to the *Xuánqiān bèijiǎn* (Complete Examination of the Mysterious Pivot), composed by the Śramaṇa Youyan of Dànqiū.
In the past, our patriarch took up the heavy responsibility of assisting in the teaching; he was one sent by the Tathāgata to perform the work of the Tathāgata—this is what is meant.
His commentary on the *Śāstra* (Shiqian) in ten fascicles is both a lexicon of terminology and a penetration of principle;

it is sufficient for those who are clever scholars to rely upon it to comprehend the *Xuánwén*, to penetrate the titles of the scriptures through the *Xuánwén*, and to reach the essential meaning of the mind through the titles, thereby entering the gate of the Ambrosia.
For this reason, there may be those among later students who, though they have not long been engaged in their studies, still find the text of the *Xuánqian* difficult to master.

Its language is obscure and difficult to cite, its reflections shadowy and brief; though one may linger between the pages of the scrolls, what leisure is there to seek out other texts to broaden one’s knowledge?
(I, the Foolish One), during the Yuanfeng era, fortunately relied upon my studies and further applied myself with vigor to investigate it;
I have thus ventured to add annotations to replace its difficulties and expand its brevity within the text.

Furthermore, I have corrected scribal errors in the transmission of the text; for this was done not only to prevent contradictions and fallacies, but also to slightly assist the beauty of the studies of later scholars.
I have divided it into four fascicles for the sake of convenient consultation and thus titled it "The Comprehensive Examination" (Beijian).
Should a discerning person read this, they will find no reason to add water to milk, cast stones into gold, or mix them together to create a deceptive display.
Preface by Chao, the Seventh Son of Heaven, New Emperor Ruijin,
upon his accession to the throne in the fifth month of the summer of the first year of the Yuanyou era, the Bingyin year; written on the day of the first waning moon,
beginning with the Jia-hermitage.
The Comprehensive Examination of the Profound Commentary, Scroll One:
Prolegomenon on the Origins,
by Junshan.
Now, the *Boshuzhi* (Records of Local Wonders) of Yuezhou states that the two daughters of the Emperor dwell on Mount Jun on Lake Dongting, calling them the "Ladies of the Xiang";
furthermore, the *Jingzhou tu yu* (Discourse on the Maps of Jingzhou) says that because it is where the Lord of the Xiang roams, it is called Mount Jun.

The *Piṇḍola-bharadvāja-vibhaṅga-śāstra* states: "Ordinary people suffer from the famine of sensual desire; because a bhikṣu eliminates this notion of craving-famine, he is called a 'remover of famine' (*piṇḍola*)."
"Pumenzi" (Son of Pumen):

"Pumen" is his name; in the following text, only the single character "Pu" (Universal) is written. Some people have offered various explanations, but it is now suspected that the character "Men" (Gate) has been omitted.
According to the preface to the *Wencangji* (Collected Works) written by Jiang Fang of Yangxian for Pumen, it says: [text follows].
Pumen’s surname was He; he was a descendant of He Yan, the former Minister of Personnel under the Wei dynasty.

His great-great-grandson was He Jie, the Magistrate of Yixing County in Changzhou. Having once competed in literary contests on the examination fields, he later withdrew his hairpin from court life to renounce worldly dust.
He resided within the abbot’s quarters of Nanyue Temple in Yuezhou, possessing nothing but Confucian texts, Buddhist scriptures, and bronze vessels.

He possessed nothing but a water jar, a mendicant’s staff, hempen robes, and hemp sandals. On the sixth day of the final month of the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era, he passed away at the monastic quarters on Mount Jun.
He was eighty-four years of age and had been a monk for forty-five years.
His disciple Tanhuan collected more than two hundred of the Master’s writings and compiled them into ten fascicles.

Regarding the composition of words and the arrangement of sounds, the *Liji* (Book of Rites), in its "Jingjie" (Explanation of the Classics) chapter, states: "The composition of words and the comparison of events is the teaching of the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals).
[They] form a sequence."
This refers to the principle of "arraying," "opening," and "closing.
In all chapters and sections concerning the various dharmas, there is opening and closing, none of which transcends the four teachings. Now, I shall first clarify the five [aggregates].
Chapter Ten: The Characteristics of the Opening and Closing of the Ten Subtleties (Jimiō Kage-no-sō). Section Five: The Opening and Closing of the Chapters, as in the first part of the *Xuánwén*.

Regarding the three kinds of opening and closing—namely, the fivefold and tenfold analogies and so forth—if one speaks of the opening and closing of the Ten Subtleties, it is like the three dharmas of mind, Buddha, and sentient beings, which are "closed" when named collectively, and "opened" when each is endowed with the Ten Subtleties.
Furthermore, the Ten Subtleties are "closed" when named collectively, while the one hundred and two [subtleties] are "opened."
The tenfold "wondrous names" as "opening" refer to the objects (*viṣaya*); the "wondrous names" as "merging" refer to the seven categories of the objects of truth (*satya-viṣaya*).

The "wondrous names" as "opening" refer to the twenty instances of wisdom; the "wondrous names" as "merging" refer to the ten instances of benefit. Other "wondrous" [categories] are to be understood by analogy.
Furthermore, the ten wondrous aspects of the Trace Gate open up the cause and merge with the fruit; the ten wondrous aspects of the Origin Gate open up the fruit and merge with the cause.
The fruit accords with the cause.
The ten sons having departed, they were consecrated [as kings];

they were deeply learned in the Dharma, cautious in their conduct, and maintained tranquility; they followed true wisdom, concealed themselves in meditative concentration, and manifested insight through their practice.
Worldly wisdom aspires to and practices the Way of tranquility; its power and insight open wide and illuminate universally, gathering all beings with pure eloquence, strong memory,
and universal manifestation of images to provide profound assistance.

The "Explanation of the Diagrams" (*Shuogua*) in the *Zhouyi* states: "In the past, when the sages created the *Yi*, they 'profoundly assisted the divine intelligence' (*youzan shenming*) and thereby produced the milfoil stalks.
Regarding "profoundly assisted," Han Kangbo says: "Profound" (*you*) means deep; "assisted" (*zan*) means to clarify.
This refers to Fuxi’s creation of the *Yi*, whereby he deeply clarified the principles of nature and destiny (*xingming*). Pumen [uses this] because Jingxi deeply clarified the Way of Zhizhe.
This is identical to the Sage’s composition of the *Yi*.
Only when the Sage has completed his work of exposition can the doubts of others be finally resolved.
The three turnings have now been completed;
formerly at Vārāṇasī, he turned the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths,
guiding and delivering beings by means of the One Vehicle.
Now he has once again turned the unsurpassed and greatest wheel of the Dharma.
The *Mong* hexagram of the *Zhou Yi* states: "It is not I who seek the ignorant youth; the ignorant youth comes to seek me. This means that it is not the child who seeks [instruction].
Because one knows where to follow yet is largely obscured, one comes to seek me in order to strike away this state of mental darkness;
hence it is said that the first six (the first line) "dispels ignorance.
Before long, one returns to the right path.
Among the many disciples of Zhiyan who were widely learned, there was Master Jingxi, through whom the Way of the Sage was not far off and was restored once again.
As the *Fu* hexagram states: "The first nine: returning before it is far; no cause for great regret."
The *Zhilixue* says: "To have the will to learn" means to be resolute in one's studies.
To rouse oneself—
"Vibrant Elevation" (zhenjǔ) means to raise [the deceased] above those who were their predecessors.

"No partiality" (wúshì)—the pronunciation of shì is identical to dí; it means "no intimacy"—as the *Lunyu* says: "There is no 'this person' and no 'that person'; the gentleman has neither intimacy nor estrangement."
"Receiving others with emptiness" refers to the hexagram Xian (Hexagram 31), which states: "The gentleman, in accordance with this, receives others with emptiness.

The commentators explain that one who wishes to influence the hearts of others must necessarily empty their own mind to receive and accommodate all things without rejecting or omitting anything. He Tao says: "Emptiness..."
To receive others with a heart that neither excludes nor rejects them, so that all things return to oneself— this is the aspiration of a gentleman.
Thus was the Zen Master of Jingxi in his compassionate reception of beings,
even when the island barbarians raised a revolt.
The one who caused the rebellion was An Lushan. Originally a man of the Hu, Lushan raised troops from Fan Yang to invade the capital.
Emperor Xuanzong fled to seek refuge in Shu. Lushan usurped the title of King of Dàyàn and occupied Luoyang, where he was subsequently killed by his son, An Qingxu.
Later, Prince Guangping led an army of one hundred and fifty thousand to punish the rebel, decapitating six million of them.
The ranks declined until the reign of Emperor Daizong, when the Western Tubo again invaded the capital, causing the common people to suffer toil and the realm to fall into chaos.
*Shùn* (pronounced with the initial *rùn*) means to follow things with one's person.
"Mian" (upper tone *min*,
lower tone *mian*) refers to looking up and down; it means to be exposed to the elements.
I take "páo" (暴) to mean "to expose," as in having no shelter from wind and rain; Mencius says, "the autumn sun exposes [all things]" (*qiūyáng yǐ pàoxī zhī*).
It is also pronounced *bó bào qiè*.
When the mind is relaxed, the achievement is doubled.
When the divine mind is at ease and leisurely, its achievements are many; as the *Book of Rites* says, "When the teacher is at ease, his achievement is doubled.
This term, "yang-yang," describes a state of profound vastness.
As for "ken-qi" (the sinews and joints), it has never been a source of painful obstruction. *Zhuangzi* records that Cook Ding said to Lord Wenhui: "What I delight in is the Way.
When I first began to butcher oxen, what I saw was nothing but whole oxen. After three years, however... [The text continues with the description of his mastery.]
"I have seen the whole ox; I encounter it with my spirit rather than looking with my eyes. I have never yet encountered a tendon, a ligament, or a knotty joint. Guo Xiang’s commentary states:
"The subtlety of the skill lies in constantly moving the blade through empty space; one has never yet struck against even the slightest obstruction.
The phonetic gloss explains: "Kěn" refers to the flesh adhering to the bone; "qǐng" refers to the place where the ox's muscle and bone intersect.
This is the point of the connection. Here, a single phrase from the *Zhuangzi* is cited to illustrate that among those who have entered the gate, there are those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).

Regarding "being ashamed that one’s person does not reach [the goal]," "reaching" means to attain. As Confucius said in the *Analects*: "In ancient times, words were not uttered until they were put into practice; they were ashamed that their persons did not reach [their words]."
The commentary states: "The ancients did not speak recklessly because their physical conduct could not keep pace [with their words].
This compares to those disciples who merely stand at the gate and retreat upon seeing the shore; they possess dull faculties."
The Great Outline does not explicitly state the meaning of the "Great Outline of the Mysterious Center" (*Xuanchong da ke*); previous masters have often failed to grasp its essential framework.
One must observe the signs to comprehend the underlying intent.
In the *Zhouyi*, the drawing of hexagrams is entirely expressed through symbols (*xiang*), such as the dragon of Qian and the horse of Kun. The *Yi* states:

"Symbols arise from intention; therefore, one may seek the intention by examining the symbols. Thus, one attains the intention by forgetting the symbols, and attains the symbols by forgetting the words. Buddhism is likewise so.
Striking upon its great joints, the ancients composed songs and chanted in harmony while striking bamboo; as the *Wenxuan* says, "The women of Han struck their rhythm.
Now, Master Pumen has composed this preface, striking out and unfolding the great principles of the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*) just like striking a rhythm.
Harmony.

Confucius, the Heavenly King, in compiling the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, recorded those who attained the orthodox line; "Heavenly King" refers to the Son of Heaven, who models himself on Heaven and practices the Way.
Therefore, he was titled the Heavenly King; "presently" refers to the Xuanzong era.

"Shanfu" (the outskirts of Shan) refers to Western Shu; "fu" means a city wall or outer enclosure. During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, he fled to Shu to escape the calamity of Lu Shan. As for the year:
It was the year of Gui-mao; the following year was Bing-chen.
"Month" (yue) refers to the month of *xiang* according to the *Erya*:
the sixth month is *qie*, the seventh month is *xiang*, and the eighth month is *mu*. "Zheng" (貞) means "correct" (*zheng*), signifying correctness.
In the seventh month. *Shiqian*,
Fascicle One, Section on Phrases and Clauses.
The character *dòu* (逗) merely completes the sense of a phrase; its meaning is explained in the commentary.

It is incorrect to cite the ancient poem’s line "In the second month, the light frost lingers in spring" (*chūndòuliú*) as an explanation for *jùdòu* (句逗), for *dòuliú* originally carries the meaning of "delaying" or "stalling," as in expressions such as "delaying and not advancing" or "lingering in the barbarian settlements."
The two masters were of the same clan, Kāśyapa; one was named Mātanga and the other was of the Zhu clan, named Dharmaratna. They were the patriarchs of the Tiantai and Jingxiu schools.

Tiantai Zhiyi, Hengyang Nan Yue, and even if there were those of the highest caliber such as Dharma Master Tai of Puzhou—who reportedly understood the sutras and śāstras on his own without having studied them under others—the people of the time said: "Pu... [The text here implies that despite such individuals, the lineage of transmission remains essential].
The Governor would not permit Daotai [to leave].
Daotai urged the assembly to refuse the appointment.
He then took leave of his disciples, saying: "In the beginning, at Waguan, forty people sat together."
When twenty people attained the Dharma, the following year over a hundred people sat together; when twenty people attained the Dharma, the following year two hundred people sat together.
It can be seen that as the number of disciples increased, those who attained the Dharma decreased by ten.
This hinders my own practice and the path of transforming others. May each of you worthy ones dwell wherever you find peace; I wish to follow my own aspiration.
"Royal Regulations" (*Wangzhi*) is the title of a chapter in the *Liji* (Book of Rites). It was compiled by the *boshi* (imperial scholars) during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Han dynasty.

Regarding the statement that "a square li constitutes a *jing*," this refers to what Mencius said: "A square li is a *jing*, consisting of nine hundred *mu*. The phrase "ten *jing* constitute a *sheng*" and so forth follows the same pattern.

According to the ancient great states, they did not exceed one hundred *li* in size. Calculating based on the allotment of one thousand chariots (*qian sheng*) for a territory of one hundred *li*, ten *jing* (well-field units) constitute one chariot;
thus, ten square *li* constitute one chariot, and one hundred square *li* constitute ten chariots.
By the method of calculating square roots, one area of one hundred square *li* consists of one hundred areas of ten square *li*. For every square [unit],...

One *shili* (ten-li square) consists of one hundred *fang-yili* (one-li squares). Its tax obligation is ten chariots. One hundred *fang-shili* (ten-li squares) thus have a tax obligation of one thousand chariots;
since the territory and the number correspond exactly, it is called "exactly one thousand chariots.
This was the scale of the Gong and Hou lords of the Xia dynasty and the states of the Yin dynasty.
Regarding the auspicious omens of the conception, the mother dreamed that five-colored fragrant smoke, light as mist, swirled around her womb; when she wished to brush it away, she heard a voice say:
"Due to the causal conditions of past lives, you have entrusted yourself to the Way of the King; merit will arrive of its own accord, so why would you cast it aside?"
Furthermore, he dreamed of swallowing white mice and other such things.
At the night of his birth,
auspicious signs appeared as a divine light filled the room and simultaneously illuminated the neighboring houses.
*Tiaochen*:
*Tiao* (pronounced as in *tiaoyao*) refers to hair just beginning to grow; *chen* (pronounced as in *chenshi*) refers to the loss of baby teeth. The *Book of Rites* states:
"A man's teeth begin to grow at eight months, and they are lost at eight years."
With sincere devotion,
he once made a vow before an image in Changsha, swearing that he would become a śramaṇa and take up the burden of the True Dharma as his own solemn responsibility.
His sincerity moved the divine, and in a dream, a Buddha image extended a golden arm to stroke the crown of his head.

Seeking the Way under his teacher, he first relied upon Vinaya Master Huikang, from whom he also mastered the Vaipulya (fangdeng) scriptures. Later, when he went to Mount Nanyue, it happened that the border between the Chen and Qi dynasties was embroiled in conflict;
disregarding his own life and valuing the Dharma above all else, he braved the perils and departed.

At the moment of death, he manifested signs, saying that Avalokiteśvara had come to welcome him; he remarked that they had been waiting for a long time for him from afar, and now that his karmic conditions were fulfilled, they would escort him at the appropriate time.
He further declared, "My rank is the fifth stage."
After his parinirvāṇa, there were miraculous responses:

some saw him emitting light, others heard the sound of a finger-snap, or those who were lame bowed down only for their feet to extend themselves on their own. They sighed in regret, lamenting that they had not heard [the Dharma] while he was alive.
Regarding the ten objects of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, once the observation of these objects is completed, the sequential order is not further proclaimed.

In the *Chanmen* (The Gate of Meditation), this is opened into ten chapters: first, the general introduction; second, the explanation of names; third, the clarification of the gates; fourth, the determination of the sequence; fifth, the mental factors; sixth, the preparatory methods; seventh, cultivation and realization;

eighth, the fruits and retributions; ninth, the arising of the teachings; and tenth, the ultimate destination. As for the three [topics] beginning with the fruits and retributions, they are likewise not explained again here.
The commentary on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* concludes with the "Buddha-path" chapter (*Fódào pǐn*); the author did not take up the brush again for the subsequent chapters.

Regarding the "Palisade Wall" (*Gōngqiáng*) analogy from the *Lúnyǔ*, Zìgòng said: "To use the metaphor of a wall, my wall, O Cí, reaches only to my shoulders; looking through it, I can see the rooms and houses within."
The Master’s love for learning is such that his wall is several *ren* high; if one does not find the gate and enter, one will not see the beauty of his ancestral temple.
The more one drills into it, the more one perceives its solidity and height.
In the *Analects*, Yan Yuan, loving the Way of Confucius, sighed deeply and said: "Looking up at it, it becomes ever higher;
drilling into it, it becomes ever more solid. Looking for it, it seems to be ahead; suddenly, it is behind.

This means that the Way of Confucius is so lofty and firm as to be inexhaustible, and so ethereal as to be beyond form or image. When one looks upward to seek it, it becomes even higher; when one drills into it...
The more one investigates it, the firmer one's conviction becomes; yet when looked upon, it seems as if it were right before one, only to suddenly appear again behind.
It is like drinking from a great river;

as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says, "It is like a thirsty person drinking from a river who does not exceed their own capacity," and as Zhuangzi says, "The dwarf mouse drinks [only a tiny amount]."
The river knows only how to fill its own belly.
[Xuanzang] Or, citing the sincere words of the sūtras and śāstras that accord with this profound and subtle [teaching],
as the Master who established the essence [of the doctrine] cited one sūtra and two śāstras, Zhizhe Zhang'an further cited Śāriputra’s entry [into the same state].
The *Dharmatā-saṃgraha* (or *Dharmatā-nāma*) and the *Mahāsūtra* state that śrāvakas perceive only emptiness and so forth;
these sincere words accord with the profound and subtle intent.
[Xuánzàng] Alternatively, various masters' differing interpretations are cited to demonstrate that they are not perfect.

As explained below in the section on the "Exposition of the School," there was a master who took provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) as the core tenet of his school. [The critique states: "Provisional means should clarify the 'three-in-three' (the three truths in each of the three aspects);
this is precisely what the present sutra rejects. How can one take that which is rejected as the core tenet?

Furthermore, another master took the untainted (*anāsrava*) among the myriad virtues as the core tenet. This was criticized as being "far too narrow" and "confused with the Lesser Vehicle's *nirvāṇa*, which is not an example of the Perfect Teaching."
In the interim, there were alternating periods of suspension,
wherein only the [lesser] teachings were set aside without being reopened, such as the suspension of the *Avataṃsaka* at the Deer Park and the suspension of three [teachings] at the Deer Park,
as will be explained in detail below.

The text is subtle when in its manifest position and clear within its latent position. Regarding the "leaving behind" and "staying" for future conditions, the *Xuánwén* (Mysterious Text) below states:
"The *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra* (Four Āgamas) accomplishes the good deeds of those in the past and explains the good deeds of those in the future."
The divination slip states: "Having completed the compilation, it is left for future generations;

as it was after, so it was before, like the lotus flower before and after. Now, to set aside the traces and establish the fundamental is to rely on the "flower before" [the teaching] according to the capacities of beings, while the "lotus" [is the realization].
It is as stated later.

If one distinguishes between the identical and the different, the seventh [chapter] says: "In a general discussion of the provisional and the real, one speaks of the fundamental and the trace; in a specific discussion of high and low, one should employ the fundamental and the trace."
Discussing truth and falsehood horizontally, one should employ the categories of the provisional and the real, the fundamental and the迹 (traces), as well as distinctions regarding the person,
the stage, wisdom, and teaching; this involves opening, abolishing, and harmonizing the three vehicles.

The opening of the dark clouds to reveal the three as one primarily concerns the principle (*li*), while the discussion of abolishing the three to reveal the one is secondary and concerns the teaching (*jiao*).

This "abolishing the teaching" (*fei jiao*) is the primary sense of abolishing the teaching; if the teaching were not abolished, the conceptualization of trees would arise again. The "converging the three to reveal the one" primarily concerns the practitioner, wherein both the person and the dharma are brought into convergence.
Regarding the mutual transformation of the three faculties and the resulting designations of "sharp" or "dull," the *Śāstra* (Commentary) states:

"In previous lives, some encountered Buddhas and heard the Dharma; among them, there were those who transformed their lower or middling faculties into superior ones and attained awakening through the *dharmaparyāya*.

There were also those who transformed their lower faculties into middling ones and gained understanding through the *aupamya-paryāya*. As for those with inferior [faculties], they did not transform [their faculties] during the three turnings."
Thus it is understood.

[Xuanzang] states: "To manifest the skillful means of the various sages, the Lord of Prophecy (Vyākaraṇa) leads forth and causes the Bodhisattvas to emerge from below, as each of these Bodhisattvas below carries [their respective marks]."
That he preaches various dharmas with a mind free from fear amidst countless retinues is his skillful means (*upāya*). Furthermore, it is said:
"I have been teaching these multitudes since long ago. This is called "revealing the origin" (*mūla-prakāśana*) by setting aside [the provisional] and pointing to the trace-gate (*vyañjana-mukha*).
Regarding Pūrṇa and others being called disciples who have "wiped away the traces," this refers to entrusting [the teaching] to them as a means to manifest the fundamental [truth].
The traces of the past reveal the essence of the present;
this is even more evident.
[The character] 積 (ji) should be written as 積 (ji).
Whether coarse or subtle, extensive or narrow,
one does not judge the two functions by taking the coarseness and narrowness of the traces as the basis for the subtlety and extensiveness of the source;
rather, this approach eliminates partiality.
The two meanings— proximity and distance in terms of analogy, and partiality and perfection in terms of phenomena—
are identical. While the Master’s intent in his preface appears at first glance to be restricted to sound,
it actually applies generally to all six sense objects and specifically to sound.
Zhang’an’s initial view seems to restrict [the term "sūtra"] to that which is designated as such by means of sound; yet,
the essence of all dharmas and all sūtras is identical.

Regarding the essence of all phenomena (*dharmas*), the subsequent text states that Vairocana pervades all places and does not transcend the Four Noble Truths, taking the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their essence.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "From the root of non-abiding, all phenomena are established.
Various sūtras employ different names for this, such as "truly good and wondrous form," "ultimate emptiness," "Tathāgatagarbha," or "the Middle Way."

The essence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) consists of those who practice through faith (*śraddhācārī*), those who practice through the Dharma (*dharmacārī*), and the essence of the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*).
The introductory section comprises five parts:
the assembly of the congregation, the manifestation of auspicious signs, the arising of doubt, the posing of questions, and the answering of questions.
The six auspicious omens:
preaching the Dharma, entering meditative absorption, raining down flowers, the earth shaking, the assembly rejoicing, and emitting light.
These are the four [instances] involving Ānanda.
Rejoicing in the Ocean of the Treasury of the Worthy (Kṣemadatta).
By using the small to gauge the large, one should likewise understand that the small [is contained within] the large.
As the *Mahāśāstra* says: "The Path-factors (mārga) open up the three liberations (vimokṣa); the three liberations open up nirvāṇa; and nirvāṇa is non-existence (abhāva)."

Furthermore, it is said that *āsravas* [outflows] are exhausted: Śrāvakas take emptiness as their object and cultivate the three gates of liberation; Bodhisattvas take the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as their object and cultivate the three gates of liberation.

This city has three gates; if one enters them, one immediately gives rise to the true path of non-outflow (*anāsrava*). The path of suppression is called the "three samādhis," and the path of abandonment is called the "three liberations.
Regarding the "Great" [Vehicle], the samādhi of emptiness within the path of suppression is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), and the signless (*animitta*) is...

The contemplation of the conventional (samvṛti) as empty, the contemplation of the wishless (apraṇihita), and the contemplation of the middle way (madhyamā-pratipad) as the path of cessation— these three gates of liberation are simply the three virtues (triguṇa). By means of the Perfect [Teaching], these three are sublated,
just as Maitreya was told to practice non-retrogression while serving as the King of Tuṣita Heaven, and so forth, up to the case of Vimalakīrti.
He rebuked [them], saying: "Do not use this dharma to entice these devaputras," and further said: "You should cause these devaputras to abandon their views that differentiate bodhi.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "The teachings on the expedient means of bodhi are without a person;

if one clings to them and does not abandon them, it constitutes an obstruction to entering the single reality (*eka-tattva*). Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "From this point onward, all preceding [views] are termed false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). This is it.
Therefore, one must abandon [the Hinayana] and so forth.

To illustrate this by refuting the Hinayana with the Perfect [Teaching], it is like when Śāriputra was sitting in meditative seclusion in the forest and Vimalakīrti rebuked him, saying: "As for true meditative seclusion, it does not consist in..."
"To manifest one's body and mind within the three realms is what constitutes 'sitting in meditation' (*yàn-zà*)"; the Commentary states:

"Śāriputra did not enter the aforementioned various *dhyānas* by means of pursuing the Buddha-wisdom; rather, he could only attain meditative absorption (*samādhi*) by staying in a quiet place, straightening his body, and withdrawing his thoughts, such that his body was like wood or stone and his mind like extinguished ashes.

Why is this so? I am old and you are young. The Buddha is endowed with wisdom and the power of abandonment; thus, I am called "old," and you are called "young."

Because the yarn is taken up by a person, one should know that each [strand] therein is capable of producing its own fruit;

Regarding the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*) and the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*), the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*), fascicle ten, quotes the *Abhidharma* as follows: "Knowledge of exhaustion refers to 'I have known suffering,' up to 'I have known the path.'"
The wisdom of non-arising means that one knows suffering and will not need to know it again, up to having cultivated the path and no longer needing to cultivate it;
this ultimate state of the true stage is called liberation. After realizing the truth, being able to explain it to others is called knowledge and vision.

Among those twenty-seven types of persons mentioned in the *Madhyama-āgama*, there are eighteen kinds of practitioners (*śaikṣa*): namely, the four candidates for the fruits (*pratipannaka*), the three who have attained the fruits (*phalastha*), those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*), the "one-interval" (*ekavicika*), and the five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*):

those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), with effort (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), without effort (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), and those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*). These constitute the eighteen. As for the remaining nine, they are the non-learners (*aśaikṣa*). Furthermore, regarding the five types of non-returners, there are those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, upon rebirth, with effort, without effort, and those who go upstream. Among these, the latter—those who go upstream—are further divided into those who do not proceed higher (*akaniṣṭhaga*) and those who do proceed higher (*bhavāgraparamaga*). Thus, including the aforementioned categories, there are twenty-seven types of persons.

The stream-enterers consist of nine types of non-learners— namely, those in the stage of falling away, the stage of preservation, the stage of reflection, the stage of abiding, the stage of penetration, the stage of immovability, the stage of non-retrogression,
those liberated by wisdom, and those liberated both ways— making twenty-seven persons in total.

Taking the 'affection for the Dharma that accords with the Path' as the cause and 'ignorance' (*avidyā*) as the condition, one gives rise to the transformation land. It further states:

it states that causes and conditions have both inverse and concordant aspects. Those that accord with birth-and-death take contaminated karma as the cause and craving, grasping, and so forth as the conditions.
Those that oppose birth-and-death take untainted right wisdom as the cause and the practice of cultivation as the condition; both serve to diminish [suffering].

When birth breaks through delusions and accords with the cycle of birth and death beyond the realms, it takes untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) as its cause and ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth as its conditions;
when it proceeds contrary to the cycle of birth and death, it takes the wisdom of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-prajñā*) as its cause and the myriad practices (*sarva-caryā*) as its conditions,
for both transform and eliminate the cycle of birth and death.
One does not disparage animals in one's mind nor harbor a haughty attitude toward them;
as will be explained in the subsequent text.

the causes and conditions of birth and death refer to those from the first bhūmi upward; "subsequent birth and death" refers to [the state] from the tenth bhūmi onward, where there is no further [birth].
Birth-and-death is itself the adamantine mind.
The Bodhisattva Wisdom-Eye asked:

Within the Āgamas, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There are four kinds of horses: first, those that are startled and alarmed upon merely seeing the shadow of the whip;

First, upon hearing that another village is subject to impermanence, one is startled; second, upon hearing that one’s own village is subject to impermanence, one develops revulsion;
third, upon hearing that one’s own kin are subject to impermanence, one develops revulsion; fourth, only when encountering one’s own illness and suffering does one finally develop revulsion.
Since the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* also employs the metaphor of four horses for birth, old age, sickness, and death, we know that both sūtras employ these as metaphors for the Three Piṭakas.

this is the very nature of the world. The remaining twenty-four principles (*tattva*) are fully detailed in those [texts] of the two, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.

moreover, it omits "contact" and "clinging," thus only describing eight factors instead of twelve. If one were to reconcile the present text from "ignorance" down to...

contact gives rise to feeling (12); feeling gives rise to craving (12); craving gives rise to grasping (12).
The twelve modes of grasping give rise to the twelve existences, and these twelve existences give rise to the twelve; thus, there are one hundred and twenty intermediate factors.

The three types of bondage refer to the states; the four types of continuity refer to the distant succession.

The latter three are merely the twelve links of dependent origination across the three periods of time, so named because they accord with the production of subsequent feelings and so forth. As for the term "a single thought-moment" (ekakṣaṇa), it does not mean an extremely brief instant;
rather, it refers to the formation of wholesome or unwholesome karma, which is termed a "single thought-moment."
In the form realm and the formless realm, there is no name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
As for "name" in the desire realm, it refers to the deluded thought at the moment of initial conception;

as for "form," it refers to the initial recognition of the two drops of the parents' fluids as one's own. It is simply because these two higher realms lack such things that [name-and-form] does not exist there.
Those who are reborn in the form realm and attain parinirvāṇa by ascending to the realm of no-remainder possess three factors that follow them from the desire realm.
Lust, sleep, and food [are the three].

the formless [continuum] continues from the formless, and form continues from form.

Regarding the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) mentioned in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the first is the body formed by entering the bliss of samādhi; this corresponds to the third and fourth [categories].
1. Because the mind is tranquil and immovable in the fifth stage (*pañcamī-bhūmi*). 2.

The body of mental transformation that realizes the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva-manomaya-kāya*), which refers to the universal entry into Buddha-fields in the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), taking the Dharma as its intrinsic nature. 3.

The body of spontaneous manifestation arising from both categories (*prakāra-dvaya-sahaja-anabhisamskāra-manomaya-kāya*), meaning that one realizes the Dharma realized by the Buddhas; both "attainment" (*siddhi*) and "birth" (*janman*) are spoken of in terms of the fruit. This is according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

Furthermore, regarding the separate classification of the stages in vertical order: although the initial text speaks of the "fifth stage," it also encompasses the seventh stage, which is the position of entering emptiness;

the eighth stage corresponds to the position of entering the provisional (the conventional). As for the phrase "congenital and innate [afflictions]," the realization of the Buddha’s realized Dharma constitutes entry into the Middle Way and belongs to the category of the Buddha;
it does not necessarily mean one has personally realized it oneself. If one were to separately connect this to the seventh stage...
Prior to the Grounds (*bhūmi*), one enters the ten distinct stages (*viśeṣa-vihāra*); from the eighth Ground onward, one enters the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).

Knowing the Buddha’s realized Dharma is the entry into *pariṇāmanā* (dedication), yet because it is not the realization of the Path itself, it is called "mind-born" (*manomaya*). This name is based on its original [meaning], and even when not joined [to the Grounds], this stage is collectively designated as such;
therefore, both are referred to as "Grounds. In the *Fuxingji* (Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra*), this is further analyzed by opening up the fifth, seventh, and ninth [stages].
Regarding the characteristics of these seeds:

that which is oriented toward saṃsāra and turned away from nirvāṇa—if one relies on the meaning of "orientation" (*ābhimukhya*) as it pertains to what has come forth, then "not deluded" constitutes the meaning of "coming forth. One ought rather to say: "That which is oriented toward nirvāṇa..."
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "pan" (棄) signifies "to turn away from," ignorance (*moha*) would then be the meaning of "to go away.
One ought rather to say that "turning away" refers to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Now, these two phrases—"facing toward" and "turning away"—are subject to doubt.

According to the Two Vehicles, the meaning is to turn away from birth-and-death and face toward *nirvāṇa*; according to the Bodhisattvas, however, the meaning is to turn away from *nirvāṇa* and face toward birth-and-death. Now...
I have not yet distinguished whether the two vehicles and bodhisattvas are oriented toward or away from [the truth];

rather, to turn one’s back on nirvana and face saṃsāra is the conventional, while to turn one’s back on saṃsāra and face nirvana is the true, thereby clarifying the Middle Way. I have briefly examined the *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* but have not yet found the relevant passage;
I request that future scholars examine it more thoroughly.
Thus, there are three types of non-existent wisdoms and many instances of the single character "non-existence" (wu).
[Xuanzang’s Commentary: From the three, two arise; from the two, seven arise, and so forth.
The commentary states: "Afflictions give rise to karma. There are three afflictions, namely ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*);

these constitute the three [links] that produce the two [subsequent links], which are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and birth (*jāti*). Furthermore, from birth arise name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the five [aggregates], as well as aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) and so forth; these constitute the two [links] that produce the seven [subsequent links].
It can be seen that the seven [links] produce the three [initial links]."
【Xuanzang’s Commentary] The *Penshi miam shushu* explains:
"The essence of dhyāna contains its constituent branches like a basin; emptiness of persons is coarse like rice, while emptiness of phenomena is subtle like flour."
"Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes see only the end but do not see the beginning"—this is the twenty-fifth passage of this Great Sūtra.
The eighth commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* explains:

"One should know that because ignorance has no root, Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes see the end but do not see the beginning; the Buddhas and Tathāgatas see both the end and the beginning. Thus it is recorded.
The commentary states: "Those who see the end among the ten stages are so called because they receive the name 'end' based on their final [attainment];
since they have severed one portion and brought that portion to an end, it is said they 'see the end. In reality, however, ignorance cannot be called an 'end.

Because the Buddha has severed the very last [portion], its subsequent manifestation is like the beginning; thus it is said he 'sees the beginning. In reality, however, ignorance cannot be called a 'beginning. If it were fixed..."

If one asks what it means for the beginning and end to be "non-abiding," if one reckons that ignorance has a beginning and an end, this is to say that the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) has a beginning and an end.
Because the entirety of *dharmatā* is definitively ignorance, and because the entire essence of ignorance is *dharmatā*.

Question: If this is so, the fault lies in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. Answer: It is not so. There is the phenomenal aspect (*事*, *vastu*) and the noumenal aspect (*理*, *tattva*). If one speaks from the perspective of the phenomenal aspect...

If one sees the beginning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one immediately sees the end of ignorance (*avidyā*); when the Buddha sees the end of the nature of phenomena, it is called seeing the beginning of ignorance.
The beginning of that which has no beginning is called the beginning of ignorance; the end of that which has no end is called the end of the nature of phenomena.
If explained according to principle, one should know that these two dharmas both begin together and end together; how much more so since these two dharmas themselves are not two distinct dharmas?

There is no beginning or end; yet, when one speaks by means of the mutual dependence between phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*), because it follows from the principle, it likewise follows from the phenomenon.

Thus, even in departing from beginning and end, it is the same. When discussing phenomena and principle in relation to that which is neither phenomenon nor principle, one speaks of "beginning and end" within that which has no beginning or end.
The text of the Great Sūtra discusses the Perfect (*yuan*) by way of the particular (*bie*); because it proceeds from the mutual dependence of phenomena, it makes this statement.

Although the eight characteristics differ, Nirvana is described through these eight characteristics called suffering—namely birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth up to the arising of the mass of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

These eight dharmas of suffering are called the "Origin" (*samudaya*); the state where these eight dharmas do not exist is called "Cessation" (*nirodha*). [The Buddha is endowed with] the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses.
Fear and so forth are called the path.

Regarding the four nutriments (*āhāra*), when edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) enters the belly, it is digested; contact-food (*sparśa-āhāra*) consists of the mutual conditioning of the three—sense organ, object, and consciousness.
When one consumes objects that are rare and desirable, there is the sense of being nourished and flourishing; this applies to consciousness throughout the three realms.
As for the food of consciousness, it is because of the powerful influence of the preceding three foods that its force subsequently increases.

Regarding the Dārṣṭāntikas (a school of masters within the Abhidharma known as the Saṃmitīya), the Vibhajyavādins explain eight types of suffering. Although there is no time at present to examine the Abhidharma texts, I shall set this forth according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

The *Śāstra* states that the Vibhajyavādins composed [this treatise]: ... [The passage continues with the detailed exposition of the eight sufferings as presented by the Vibhajyavādins. ... Thus it is said. The *Vibhāṣā* further explains: "The Vibhajyavādins maintain that there are eight kinds of suffering. It is stated: "The Vibhajyavādins composed [the following]: [and so on].
Thus it is said: if there are eight aspects of suffering, these are suffering and the truth of suffering; other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are suffering but not the truth of suffering.
Craving that brings about future existence (*punarbhava*) is the origin and the truth of the origin; other cravings and other causes of contamination are the origin but not the truth of the origin.

The exhaustion of the craving that brings about future existence is cessation (*nirodha*); the exhaustion of other cravings and other contaminated phenomena is [cessation but] not the truth of cessation.
The exhaustion of causes is cessation, but it is not the Truth of Cessation; the training in the Eightfold Path is the Path, and it is the Truth of the Path.
Other trained dharmas (*śaikṣa-dharma*) and all untrained dharmas (*aśaikṣa-dharma*) are the Path, but they are not the Truth of the Path.

If one were to say that Arhats accomplish only the two truths of Suffering and Cessation, but do not accomplish the two truths of Origination and the Path—for what reason? [Because] it would entail...

Because the craving for future existence has already been completely eradicated by Arhats, and because they have already abandoned [all factors] when attaining the fruit of Arhatship through the training in the Eightfold Path, the treatise does not explain why other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are not the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Now, let us resolve this: since it mentions "Arhats," it likely refers to Arhats in relation to themselves and others.
If one must examine the truths with truthfulness, and if one considers other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as suffering belonging to others rather than to oneself,
then one studies by distinguishing between self and other regarding everything from the truth of suffering up to the truth of the path.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Wénjù Shì) explains:

"If the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) is the eye, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is wisdom; if the subsequent patience (*anvayakṣānti*) is clarity, the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is awakening.
This applies likewise to the remaining three truths; thus, sixteen moments of mind are established. Those of the three faculties each attain these sixteen."
This constitutes forty-eight lines.
To know the sense bases (*āyatana*) as gateways, and so forth, as stated in other sūtras such as those on the Truth of Suffering:
"To know the sense bases as gateways is also called suffering; this is termed intermediate wisdom that discriminates the sense bases."
That there are immeasurable marks, all of which are suffering and not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—this is called superior wisdom.
Even up to the knowledge that discriminates marks—this is called middling wisdom.
That one discriminates that consciousness has immeasurable marks and this is not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—this is called superior wisdom. Regarding such meanings as these, I...

That sutra also does not mention it (the phrase "knowing the elements in the interim" and "knowing that form, feeling, perception, and formations are all fetters" is called middle wisdom; the passage "discerning the various elements have immeasurable characteristics and so forth" is called superior wisdom—examples such as these can be understood from the preceding and following context).
Furthermore, knowing that the causal conditions of craving can give rise to the five aggregates is called middle wisdom.
[Knowing] that a single person gives rise to infinite and boundless feelings, which cannot be known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and being able to know all [of them], is called superior wisdom.
Such cravings as these that arise in sentient beings are called "superior wisdom.
Because I did not explain such meanings in that sutra, I have now annotated the remainder here. As in the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Cessation, which cannot be calculated;
and in the Truth of the Path, there are likewise two phrases—immeasurable and boundless—under both of which it says: "not for the sake of all sounds."
That which is known by the Pratyekabuddhas is called "superior wisdom. Regarding such meanings as these, I did not explain them in that sutra;
because their meaning is identical to that of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), I merely noted: "as in the Truth of Suffering."
The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
the conventional truth is itself suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), while the ultimate truth is the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*). The twelfth [chapter] states:

"The aggregation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is designated by the name 'so-and-so,' an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). According to that designation, this is called conventional truth; [this is] the explanation of the aggregates."

"There is no person with such-and-such a name who exists apart from the aggregates, nor is there a person with such-and-such a name who appears in the world, who can be known according to their intrinsic nature and characteristics;
this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)," and so forth. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha:
"If that which is true is taken as the true truth, then the dharma of reality is itself the Tathāgata, the Buddha of empty space."
If the nature [of things] were thus, there would be no distinction between the Tathāgata, space, and the Buddha-nature.
The Buddha said: "Mañjuśrī, there is suffering, there is the truth, and there is reality; even up to: there is the path, there is the truth, and there is reality.
Good son, the Tathāgata is neither suffering nor the truth, yet he is real. Space is neither suffering nor the truth, yet it is real. The Buddha-nature is neither..."

"Suffering is not the truth, yet it is real" (and so forth). Regarding "neither suffering nor truth, yet it is real," this refers to the fourfold application of the four truths through the subtle middle-way wisdom.
This is explained extensively as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
There is one redundant character, "shi" (釋).
The term "tong" (通) in "yuanpo tongdeng" (圓破通等) should be changed to "bie" (別).

The sequence of the sūtra text does not follow the order of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. It states: "Since one cannot even find that all dharmas tend toward the provisional form, how could there be tending toward or not tending toward emptiness or the middle?"
In the various texts, the meaning is established by using the single phrase "all phenomena produced through causes and conditions" from the *Śālistamba-sūtra* as the primary proof;
the subsequent sections of the text naturally comprise two chapters belonging to the *Piṭaka*.
The Chapter on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination and the Chapter on Refuting Erroneous Views state that true speech is [identical to] false speech;

the subsequent text says, "Because one gives rise to views through speech, birth and death are vast and boundless. The *Zhǎnshì* (Commentary) explains: "The essence of the teaching is fundamentally real; for all..."
Because the dogmatic views born of emotional attachment take afflictions as their cause, the fruit of suffering remains vast and unceasing.

It is further said that although the true reality is subtle, it becomes coarse through attachment—just as the view of "middle" differs from the view of "extremes," and the view of "emptiness" differs from the view of "existence."

In the preceding section on "Abolishing Expedient Contemplation" (*fèiquán guān*), it was first established by correlating the sequential three contemplations (*cìdì sānguān*) vertically with the four sets of the Four Noble Truths;

next, the single-mind three contemplations (*yīxīn sānguān*) were correlated comprehensively with the four sets of the Four Noble Truths. Thus, the former "abandoned contemplation" is considered coarse, while the subsequent "opened contemplation" is considered sublime.
The simultaneous opening and ceasing [of the two truths] are observed as one in essence.
[Xuanzang’s Commentary: The *Sūtra on the Sublime Samādhi* records that the Buddha said:
"In the past, I debated the Two Truths with Mañjuśrī; because of this, we both fell into the three miserable realms. This sūtra does not exist [in the current canon].
For a measure of kalpas, I swallowed iron balls and emerged from hell, where I encountered Kāśyapa Buddha, who explained for me the two truths of existence and non-existence.
Kāśyapa Buddha said: "All dharmas lack any fixed nature; your assertion of existence and non-existence is incorrect.
All dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent; as for these two truths, they are both existent and non-existent."
"You only know the words but do not understand their meaning.

[Xuán] states that the "two births" of the Bodhisattva are now judged in the *Xuánwén* to belong to the Śrāvaka of the Tripiṭaka; however, in the *Fǔxíng*, it clarifies the two births of the Mahāyāna.

The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states that there are four different types of wisdom for observing causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and that through these differences, one attains various forms of bodhi.

When these words were spoken, ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the true reality (*bhūtataṭva*) of a single birth, and five thousand bodhisattvas attained the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of two births.
Zhiyan’s commentary explains: "The three vehicles equally observe the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), yet their wisdom and understanding differ."

The "one life" and "two lives" refer to the breaking of the first and second grades of ignorance; the true reality (*dharmatā*) is the distinct principle (*bhedārtha*), while the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna-artha*).
This refers to those of sharp faculties who enter the distinct and perfect teachings, and having broken through ignorance, attain Buddhahood through the eight aspects;

this is the meaning of the Buddha-fruit appearing externally. However, by observing the various sutras, one realizes that attaining the Way at the conclusion of the assembly is precisely what one must know.
The meaning of "shared" and "distinct," as well as the small and great kalpas of birth, are distinguished by scholars.

Since both the beginning of the *Prathama-kalpa* (Initial Kalpa) and the beginning of the *Prathama-asamkhyeya* (First Incalculable Aeon) are termed "prior to that," there is room for the possibility that falling [into a lower realm] occurs within the first *asamkhyeya*—
which, according to common discourse, is situated outside the stage of ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*)— while the second *asamkhyeya* [is situated within it].

If one is already in the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) during the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, and even in the initial stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) during the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*— both of which belong to the outer ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*)—
one still risks falling back, how much more so before those stages?
Why must it be that one only departs from the evil realms at the end of the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*?
The *Jizhu yi* (Record of the Essential Meaning) states: "At the beginning of the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, one has already abandoned the five obstacles;

why must one wait until the end? Regarding the meaning of abandoning these obstacles, there are three differing explanations. Within the Small Four Teachings (*xiǎo sìjiào*), it is said that this occurs at the start of the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa. However, the commentary (*qiān wén*) here states it is at the beginning of the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, one only abandons the five obstacles at the time of cultivating the marks of a Great Man (*lakṣaṇa-karman*) during the hundred kalpas [of the final stage].
Therefore, the treatise states: "From the Bodhisattva who practices these deeds, one obtains the name 'born in a happy realm,' endowed with noble lineage, male form, mindfulness, and firm resolve.
One should observe evil companions and evil associates.
The character "friend" (you) is a scribal error in the sutra; it should read "contemplating evil elephants.
Regarding "evil associates" (pāpamitra), the sutra states that they destroy immeasurable bodies;
within the scripture, it specifies that they destroy immeasurable virtuous bodies.

The foul body and the pure body are like evil elephants that can destroy the impure body; the evil spiritual friend is like an evil elephant that can destroy the pure body; the physical body is like an evil elephant that can destroy the fleshly body;
and the evil spiritual friend is like [an evil elephant] that can destroy the Dharma-body.
[Xuán] Míng [Zhì] maintains that the Buddha-fruit transcends the two truths;

Fǔxíng and Zhuāngyán maintain it does not transcend them. Kāishàn maintains it does not transcend them because Bodhisattvas—among those who train in the Three Vehicles—possess both the "exclusive" and "non-exclusive" [paths].
Ancient scholars did not understand the distinction between the two faculties of sharp and dull, but merely debated whether the Buddha-fruit transcends [the two truths] or not.

Since the intent behind the opening and closing [of the gates] has not yet been seen in the *Chū* (the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra*), we know that the two schools each grasp only one side of the present text— either the sharp or the dull faculty—
and still do not understand that the text goes beyond this to separately illuminate the realm of the Middle Way, whereby one employs the wisdom of the Middle Way to advance and shatter ignorance.
If one cannot understand this, those of dull faculties rely on the teaching and realize the truth together with the followers of the Two Vehicles.

One should know with certainty that each of the two masters has grasped a partial meaning; if one grasps the present meaning, then whether [the teaching] is issued forth or not, the principles are all fully established.
[Xuanzang]: Advancing, it does not constitute three; retreating, it does not constitute two.

If those of sharp faculties who have attained the Separate and Perfect [teachings] were to receive only the teaching of the two truths, and it were said that there is no distinct principle to be illuminated outside of these two truths, this would be an advancement for them but not a penetration of the three—Separate, Perfect, and [Shared]—and thus a loss.

Furthermore, if they were to illuminate the distinct principle [of the Separate], yet regress from it, this would be a loss regarding the two dharmas of the fruit-Buddhas of the Treasury and Shared [teachings]. Such are the errors of advancing and retreating.

[Xuanzang’s Commentary]: Regarding the clarification of the two truths based on the four provisional designations (*prajñapti*), the *Mahā-śāstra* discusses only three provisional designations. As for the mention of "four," some say that the provisional designation of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*) has not yet been seen in its source.
If one refers to the twenty-three schools, then Guangzhai, Jingtuō, Huichao, and various princes each consulted with two [masters].
The Truths are luminously clear, and the Luminous One answered them all.

Among the ten powers of faculties and inclinations (*indriya-vīrya-daśabala*), the power of faculties (*indriya-bala*) refers to the Buddha’s knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of other sentient beings.
Regarding the lower characteristic, "thoroughly knowing the power of desire as it truly is": the Buddha thoroughly knows the various desires of other sentient beings as they truly are;
this cannot be destroyed and cannot be surpassed.
Just as the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), though adjacent to the Truth (*satya*), still possesses many grades.
Just as among the disciples of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, some are superior while others are inferior;
[Xuanzang’s version: Small clouds arise to obstruct great clouds, and clouds are able to obscure the moon;

this is a metaphor for how afflictions can obstruct the Truth. When the clouds disperse and the moon is seen, the obstructions are extinguished and wisdom becomes pure. This is what is meant by "arising."
"Kai" (open) refers to the names of non-Buddhist outsiders such as the Kālavāda;

those who are refuted by the Initial Teaching all possess the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*), and for this reason it is called "long."
The *Āgama* refutes the non-Buddhists;
this is the ninth section on the various worldly sentiments,
titled "The Sūtra on the Production of Many Thoughts," which is contained within the "Chapter on Noble Conduct."
Regarding the *Loka-sūtra*, the *Pada-sūtra*, the *Bandha-sūtra*, and so forth:

what is meant by "world" (*loka*)? It refers to things such as men, women, jars, clothing, vehicles, and houses. What is meant by "phrase" (*pada*)? It refers to things such as the four lines of a single verse.
What is meant by "binding" (*bandha*)? It refers to things such as rolling up, joining, tying, binding, and placing the palms together.
What phenomena are like the world? It is like the striking of a gong to assemble the sangha, the beating of a solemn drum, or the blowing of a horn to signal the time.
How does one become attached? It is like a person looking at someone from afar wearing dyed robes; they conceive a perception and become attached, saying, "This is a śramaṇa, not a brāhmaṇa.
Seeing someone with knotted cords crossed over their body, they immediately form the thought, "This is a brāhmaṇa."
The "gate" is not a śramaṇa.
The five worldly dharmas differ in name from those mentioned previously;
they differ from such things as the self (ātman), sentient beings (sattva), and the horns of a rabbit.
[Xuanzang]: For example, when taking cessation as an object, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) arise within the Four Truths;
although cessation itself is not originally a cause-condition for the latent dispositions, it nevertheless gives rise to the seven latent dispositions.
How extensive are the scriptures in the Western Regions?

That commentary states: "In foreign sutras, there are many instances of 'crossing over' (tú) and few of 'measuring' (liàng). This is merely the Master of Records (Jìzhǔ) having rephrased the language.

Regarding the passage in the *Jīngēngyè jīng* that says, "I now have much gold, silver, and so forth," the commentary explains: "Gold refers to the principle of the Separate Teaching (biéjiào), while silver refers to the Common Teaching (tōngjiào)."
The ultimate truth discussed in the "Great Chapter on Doctrine" (Shastric Section) does not transcend these two.
As stated in the commentary regarding the three cycles, each has its own distinct name;
the first cycle is called the "Dharma-Exposition" (dharmadeśanā), which generally encompasses all three [aspects], like the udumbara flower that appears but once in an aeon.

The "manifesting of the ear" is an explanation by way of analogy (*aupamya*). "If I encounter sentient beings, I teach them all the Buddha-way" is an explanation by way of cause and condition (*nidāna*);
among these, "the specific names" refers to the particular [teachings], while "analogy" refers to the general [teachings], both of which likewise possess the three modes of exposition.

My previous statement that "all are for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas" is the explanation by way of the Dharma (*dharma-nirdeśa*). "Under twenty thousand Buddhas, I have constantly taught and transformed you" is the explanation by way of cause and condition. Below...
Zhou Tong also possesses the three assemblies and is further purified, being led into the Buddha-wisdom; this is the discourse on the Dharma.

"There is one guide" is the discourse through parable. As for why these three cycles are established, it is because they follow what is prevalent and what is fundamental, so that their names do not become confused, each being based upon a single meaning.
【Xuanzang] From this point on, one version reads "one path" (yītú).
This refers to the passage in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra* that analyzes the three provisional designations (*trividha-prajñapti*) within the context of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

The Tripiṭaka is categorized as the three provisional designations according to phenomena (*dharma*), while the three teachings of the Mahāyāna gate are categorized as the three provisional designations according to principle (*tattva*).
Master Sōng of Pengcheng Temple in Xuzhou said:
"A Buddha should not remain permanently; at the time of his final passing, his tongue would have perished first."

The *Sūtra on the Eight Impure Things Permitted for Storage* states that the prohibitions regarding storage do not exceed eight types, all of which are termed "impure": first, fields, houses, and gardens;
second, cultivated plants; third, stored grain and silk; fourth, keeping male and female servants; fifth, tethering and raising birds and beasts; sixth, money and precious gems.
7. Precious objects: felt rugs and blankets; 8. Vessels: cauldrons and pots; 9. Furnishings: elephant-ivory and gold-adorned couches with headboards.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* clarifies ten kinds of superior characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), which are divided into ten chapters:
first, the superior characteristic of the basis (*āśraya-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), namely the pure and impure dharmas, which is based upon the *ālayavijñāna*; second, that which is to be known...
The excellence of the characteristics of what is to be known (*jñeya-lakṣaṇa-viśeṣa*) refers to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) that are to be known as the delusions.

The excellence of the characteristics of the entry into what is to be known (*jñeya-praveśa-lakṣaṇa-viśeṣa*) refers to knowing that the three natures can constitute both the entry and that which is entered, namely, consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

The excellence of the characteristics of the cause and fruit of the entry (*praveśa-hetu-phala-lakṣaṇa-viśeṣa*) refers to the fact that the cause of entering consciousness-only consists of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) during the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), while the fruit of the entry is the transformation [of the basis] achieved within that same stage of penetration.
The result consists of five aspects: first, the distinction of the excellence of the cultivation of cause and effect;

this refers to the six perfections and four virtues within the ten stages, such as the Joyous Stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), wherein each stage possesses its own specific distinctions. Sixth, regarding the distinction of cultivation, there is the excellence of the precepts;

this refers to all forms of discipline within the ten stages, characterized by the non-commission of any evil. Seventh, regarding the excellence of the training in the mind, it refers to that which relies upon... [the text continues].
1. The superior characteristic of the training in wisdom based on the cultivation of sublime meditative concentration refers to taking wisdom as the basis, which is non-conceptual knowledge.
2. The superior characteristic of the result of the nine trainings, which is cessation, refers to the specific knowledge of cessation, which is precisely non-abiding nirvana.
3. The superior characteristic of the differentiation of knowledges refers to the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which is free from all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and obstacles.

(As stated above) The original treatise consists of three fascicles composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; within this treatise, the ten supreme characteristics (*daśa-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) are divided into ten chapters and explained one by one.

Furthermore, Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed a commentary on it in twelve fascicles, and there is also an exegetical commentary (*vyākhyā*) in eight fascicles, totaling twenty-three fascicles. All of these clarify the meaning of the ten supreme characteristics. [End of] Preface.
Regarding the three natures: first, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); second, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); and third, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The dependent nature refers to the dependent-arising nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is the basis upon which consciousness alone truly exists, appearing as if it were external objects.
Why is it called "dependent"? For what reason and conditions is it termed "dependent-arising"?
That which arises from seeds perfumed by itself is called "dependent origination" (paratantra-svabhāva);
because it lacks the capacity to abide spontaneously after the initial moment, it is termed "dependent. Second, regarding the "imagined nature" (parikalpita-svabhāva):

this refers to the grasping of the marks of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that gives rise to inverted cognition; one must consider what objective realm is apprehended, what characteristics are grasped, and by what conditions it is established.
"Reality is twofold" refers to the thoroughly established nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) being pure; the above constitutes the text from the *Xuanzang* commentary.

Regarding the "inconceivable fourfold negation of attachment," it was previously stated that the mind of ignorance is not self-originated, not other-originated, not co-originated, and not without cause; thus, none of these four propositions apply.
If there are causes and conditions for the four *siddhāntas*, it may also be explained as follows:
first, "one-three-one-three.
This means that when cessation (*śamatha*) takes the truths (*satya*) as its object, one truth becomes three truths; and when the truths are bound to cessation, [the same occurs].

One cessation is three cessations; for example, although there are three characteristics within a single moment of mind, though it is a single moment of mind, it possesses these three characteristics.
It is the same with cessation and the truths (*satya*): although the phenomena that are ceased are one, they are three;
and although the minds that cease them are three, they are one. When observing an object through observation, a single object becomes three objects; as the object gives rise to [the observation]...
Contemplation is such that a single contemplation constitutes three contemplations.
This is the Tathāgata’s space-like buddha-nature.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī: "The ultimate truth is called the True Dharma; it is also called that which is devoid of falsehood. Furthermore, [it is]...
It is named the Great Vehicle, and it is also called the Single Path, pure and without duality.
That which possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity is termed the True Reality (*satya*). Mañjuśrī raised an objection, saying:

"If true reality constitutes the True Reality, then the true nature of phenomena is the Tathāgata, space, and Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). If this is so, then the Tathāgata, space, and Buddha-nature..."

There is no distinction [between them]. The Buddha says that there is suffering, there is the truth of suffering, there is reality; there is accumulation, there is the truth of accumulation, there is reality;
there is cessation, there is the truth of cessation, there is reality; there is the path, there is the truth of the path, there is reality.

Good son, the Tathāgata is neither suffering nor the truth of suffering, yet he is reality; empty space is neither suffering nor the truth of suffering, yet it is reality; the Buddha-nature is neither suffering nor the truth of suffering, yet it is reality.
Mañjuśrī said: "That which is called suffering has the characteristic of impermanence and the characteristic of being subject to cessation;
this is the ultimate truth. The nature of the Tathāgata is neither suffering, nor impermanent, nor subject to cessation; therefore, it is the ultimate reality.
The Buddha-nature of empty space is not like that."

In the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the Venerable Pūrṇa stated that the four truths—namely, conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—are likewise difficult to comprehend. Now, based on the *Vibhāṣā*, [the following] is set forth:
Section 77 states that the Venerable Pārśva said: "The 'one truth' refers to each of the four noble truths being singular; that is, suffering is exclusively one."
Because there is no second truth among the truths from suffering up to the path, and because there is only one path with no second path, it is said that there is "one truth.
This does not contradict the teaching of four truths. Furthermore, the term "one truth" refers to the single Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), intended to exclude other notions of liberation;
for various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) speak of four liberations, namely the four spheres of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.). Furthermore, it is said:
The one truth refers to the single Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), which is intended to exclude other [false] paths to truth; for various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) propound many paths to truth,
such as fasting as the path, lying in ashes as the path, drinking wind or water,

eating fruit or vegetables, remaining naked, sleeping on thorns, or else maintaining a vow not to lie down, wearing tattered rags, taking medicinal drugs, or practicing self-mortification through fasting.
Taking food and such as the path is likewise not the path; if the Buddha speaks of the true path, he refers to the Noble Eightfold Path beginning with Right View.
Furthermore, "one truth" refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), because it eternally abandons all suffering of birth and death.
Again, "one truth" refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), because it is able to sever all causes of birth and death.
In other sūtras it is said that there are two truths: first, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and second, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
What is the meaning of this? Some explain it as follows: among the four truths, the first two are conventional truths;

things such as men and women, walking and staying, as well as jars and robes, are conventional matters included within the two truths of suffering and its origin. The latter two truths are the ultimate.
The ultimate meaning, the various emergences, the provisional, and the true merits are all subsumed within the two truths of the Path and Cessation.
Furthermore, some say that the first three truths are conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), because within the truths of Suffering and its Origin there are conventional phenomena.
The Buddha taught that the Truth of Cessation is like a city, like a palace, like the further shore, and so forth; such conventional designations exist within the Truth of Cessation as well.
Therefore, the Truth of Cessation is also called conventional; the Truth of the Path alone is both ultimate and conventional.
Since these [other truths] are not conventionally established therein, the commentator says: all four truths possess both conventional and ultimate aspects.

Regarding the conventional aspect within the Truth of Suffering, the meaning is as previously explained. As for the ultimate aspect within suffering, it refers to suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
Within the principle of origination (*samudaya*), that which is ultimate refers to the arising of phenomena through causes and conditions;
within the principle of cessation (*nirodha*), that which is conventional refers to what the Buddha taught regarding the truth of cessation as being like a garden, a forest, or the further shore.

Within cessation, that which is ultimate refers to cessation as peace, excellence, and renunciation; within the path (*mārga*), that which is conventional refers to what the Buddha taught regarding the truth of the path as being like a boat or a raft.
The stone is like a mountain, like a ladder, like a bench, like a platform, like a pavilion, like a flower, and like a watercourse.
Within these paths, that which is ultimate (paramārtha) refers to the path as the act of walking out, and so forth, up to the statement: "The Venerable Vasumitra has stated thus:
'That which manifests names is the conventional (saṃvṛti); the dharma manifested is the ultimate. He further states: 'It conforms to the world.'"
That which is spoken of as "name" is the conventional; that which is spoken of in accordance with the noble ones is the ultimate. Furthermore, the Great Virtuous One said:
