【Xuanzang】If the Blessed One teaches that suffering and its origin are to be trusted and revered, those who are ready for conversion will accept them.
This first phrase is abbreviated in the following text; according to the *Śāstra*, it adds the phrase "and then they think as follows" to make the meaning easier to understand.
The *Śāstra* says: "If the Buddha teaches suffering and its origin, they then think: 'Since beginningless time, I have been [bound] by this.'"
Since base afflictions, unwholesome conduct, and their resulting fruits cause such turmoil and oppression, how could one possibly find faith or delight in them?

However, when it is said that these are extinguished through the Path, one develops deep faith and delight, desiring not to abandon it; therefore, within this context, the Path and Cessation are discussed specifically.

[Xuanzang’s Commentary] The *Jinxin silun* (Treatise on the Full Faith in the Four Truths) states that there are two kinds of faith: first, faith in what is possible; second, faith and delight in the Path and Cessation (*mārga-nirodha-satya*). These two kinds of faith are both present regarding the Truths of Cessation and the Path.

Although there is no "faith and delight" regarding the Truths of Suffering and Origination (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*), there is "faith in what is possible"; therefore, the Truths of Suffering and Origination are likewise [objects of faith].
Because it gives rise to faith, the Venerable Pārśva said that the Path and Cessation are praised for the purpose of wearying one of Suffering and its Origin;
that is to say, this Path and Cessation are tranquil, sublime, peaceful, and remedial, as they counteract the inferior, base, and loathsome phenomena of Suffering and its Origin.
[Xuanzang’s Commentary]: Regarding these three stages, there are many obstacles.
The treatise states that during these three stages, various karmas and afflictions create extreme obstacles for the practitioner.

This means that from the time one enters the stages of *mūrdhan* (Summits) and *kṣānti* (Patience), the karmas and afflictions capable of inducing rebirth in the evil destinies become extreme obstacles. This is the intended meaning.
If a practitioner enters the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), they will no longer undergo rebirth in the miserable destinies; for which body would they receive the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*)?

When these two types of noble ones (*ārya*) become free from the defilement of desire, their karma and afflictions that could induce birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are rendered utterly obstructed.
This means that if a practitioner becomes free from the defilement of desire, they will certainly never again undergo birth in the desire realm.

Regarding the phrase "in whose body one experiences the ripening fruit": when one attains the three fruits up to Arhatship, the karmas and afflictions that could induce future existence become extremely obstructed.
This means that if one attains the fruit of Arhatship, one will certainly not undergo further birth and death;
thus, the question "in whose body one experiences the ripening fruit" and so forth is merely rhetorical.
Nor can one give rise to the acquisition of non-acquisition; because one contemplates suffering,
one gives rise to the acquisition of the capacity to acquire that [contemplation] regarding suffering and so forth.
The Commentary states: "Because one contemplates suffering, one is able to give rise to and cultivate those four aspects [of the Truth of Suffering] that follow it.
In the current text, there is an extra character "得" (to obtain/attain).
All [these aspects] have wisdom as their essence.

The *Śāstra* states: "All are wisdom; the five [aggregates] excluding acquisition (*prāpti*) constitute their essential nature. This means that the four stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth have wisdom as their essential nature.

If one includes their associated factors (*sahabhū*), they consist of the five aggregates in nature. (The commentary on that passage states: "There is the morality coexistent with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*), which constitutes the aggregate of form; the remaining four [aggregates] are to be understood accordingly.

Within these four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*)—Heat and the others—there is an "acquisition" (*prāpti*) that acts as an associated factor; however, this acquisition is not itself the essential nature of the four roots of goodness such as Heat.
Therefore, it is said that with the exception of "attainment" (*prāpti*) and so forth, the rest is the same as the text of the *Śāstra*.
Starting from the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), one patience (*kṣānti*) and one knowledge (*jñāna*) arise;

observing the object of the Truth of Suffering in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), there arises the untainted (*anāsrava*) [wisdom] that severs the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) below suffering, which is called the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*).

The first mind is *kṣānti* (patience). Next, the arising of a single moment called *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* (knowledge of the dharma of suffering), which is the unconditioned state of cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), is the second mind.
Next, observing the suffering of the higher realms, the stage called *duḥkha- anvaya-kṣānti* (subsequent patience regarding suffering) is the third mind;

by severing the afflictions of the two upper realms and realizing the principle of cessation, it is the fourth mind, *duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge regarding suffering). Next, one observes the origin (*samudaya*) of the desire realm.

The patience regarding the dharma of origin (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*) is called the fifth mind; the knowledge of the dharma of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*) is called the sixth mind. Next, one contemplates the origin of the higher realms;

the subsequent patience regarding the category of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-kṣānti*) is called the seventh mind, and the subsequent knowledge of the category of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) is the eighth mind. Next, one contemplates the cessation of the desire realm;

the subsequent patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*) is called the ninth mind, and the subsequent knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) is called the tenth mind. Next, one contemplates the cessation of the higher realms...
The eleventh moment of mind is called the "patience of the subsequent knowledge of cessation" (*nirodha-anvaya-kṣānti*); the twelfth moment of mind is called the "subsequent knowledge of cessation.

Next, observing the path of the desire realm, it is called the "dharma-patience of the path" (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*), which is the thirteenth moment of mind; the fourteenth moment of mind is called the "dharma-knowledge of the path" (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*).

Next, observing the path of the higher realms, it is called the "subsequent patience of the path" (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*), which is the fifteenth moment of mind; then, one moment arises for a single instant.
The path-subsequent knowledge (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) is called the sixteenth moment of consciousness.
[Xuanzang’s Commentary: It eliminates all paths collectively;
both the upper and lower paths, as well as their objects and modes of activity, are simultaneously removed.
[Xuanzang’s Commentary]: "The retinue of the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) is inseparable from it.

From the phrase "cannot surpass the vision of the truths" down to "how much less the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*)," this collectively explains the merits of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), meaning that even the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) cannot surpass it.
Regarding "the retinue of the vision of the truths," the *Śāstra* states: "that which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*)."
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is an attendant of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and is subordinate to it;

its wisdom-power is superior [to that of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), which is the subject hereafter]. This dharma, however, is not so. Furthermore, how could it surpass the meditative absorption of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇabhāvanā*)?

Yet those attainments (*samāpatti*) and the rebirths they induce are not shared with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); this dharma, however, is not so. Moreover, how could it surpass the first moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
Furthermore, when those roots of goodness are cultivated, they are free from all obstacles and their basis is purified; this dharma is not so.
Moreover, how could it surpass the samādhis of emptiness-emptiness, wishlessness-wishlessness, and signlessness-signlessness?
For those [samādhis] are still able to bring about revulsion toward the Noble Path, let alone toward that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*); this dharma is not so.
Having first attained the fourth dhyāna through perfuming, one again causes many moments of uncontaminated (anāsrava) states to arise in succession;
from this, many moments of contaminated (sāsrava) states are induced, and from these, many moments of uncontaminated states arise once more. In this manner, they gradually decrease.
From the initial stage up to the final two moments of untainted (anāsrava) consciousness, they are followed by the production of two moments of tainted (sāsrava) consciousness;
immediately thereafter, two moments of untainted consciousness are produced again. This process of alternating and perfuming constitutes the completion of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Following this, there is a single moment of untainted consciousness, then another single moment of tainted consciousness, and immediately after that, one moment of untainted consciousness is produced; this is termed the "fundamental" (*maula*) state.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "It is accomplished by a single moment of intermingling" (and so forth). "Intermingled perfuming" (*jia xun*) refers to when there are outflow-free moments before and after, with outflowing moments in between;
because many such moments of outflow are rendered into a single moment of outflow-free [mind], it is said that they arise through "intermingled perfuming.
Regarding the generation of the five categories, this is due to the gradations in the perfumed dhyānas, namely: inferior, middling, superior, further superior, and the utmost superior.

This is the contemplation of counting the breaths (*ānāpānasmṛti*). The Sūtra says: "An" means arising; "Pan" means cessation. The fundamental dhyānas arise from counting the breaths. [Xuanzang’s Commentary]:
Relying on the *anāgamya* (preparatory stage) is the most basic; relying on the first dhyāna is superior; the intermediate state is extensive.

Regarding the "not-yet-attained concentration" (*anāgamya-samādhi*): after the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there occurs a sudden, total transformation wherein one no longer perceives the body, head, clothing, or bedding within that desire-realm concentration;
it is as if they were empty space. This physical state constitutes a hindrance (*āvaraṇa*).

When this hindrance is removed and the body becomes empty, one attains what is called the "not-yet-attained" concentration. According to the *Chanmen* (The Gate of Dhyāna), between the first and second dhyānas, and between the second and third dhyānas, there are both intermediate stages (*antara-bhūmi*).
In this present text, that which exists between the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna is called the "intermediate" (dhyānāntara).
Master Miao-yin says that it may be added as the seventh [stage], based on the body of the desire realm;
the commentary states: "Master Miao-yin says that the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan* are based on all seven stages, whereas regarding the preceding six stages, they have not yet arisen."

Regarding the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*) and the four dhyānas, there are nine additional bases when including the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), based on a body within the desire realm. (This concludes the discussion in the treatise.

This refers to the four stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth arising based on the bodies of humans and devas in the desire realm—excluding the human destiny of Uttarakuru and including the three continents and the six heavens of the desire realm.

These arise in nine locations; they arise based solely on those in the desire realm because only such beings are capable of generating revulsion toward suffering. Thus, the first three [levels] are wholesome.
The four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*) first arise in the three continents; subsequently, they continue to manifest even in the six heavens.

Furthermore, the fourth root of goodness also arises for the first time among the gods, because each of these four roots of goodness lasts for only a single moment of thought. Therefore, they can first arise within both the human and celestial realms.

Regarding the three realms, women can attain two of them (this restates the treatise). These four roots of goodness depend solely upon those who are male or female, and not upon *ṣaṇḍha* (eunuchs), etc. (*ṣaṇḍha*)...
[This refers to] a eunuch. Regarding the statement that "the three preceding roots of goodness are acquired as two by both men and women, and furthermore, men acquire two":

this means that a man acquires both the male root of goodness and the female root of goodness; and that a woman acquires both the female root of goodness and the male root of goodness. Thus they are said to "acquire two.
This is because when those in the stages of *ūṣmagata* and so forth undergo a change of gender—men transforming into women or women transforming [into men]—they acquire both.
Regarding the statement: "For a male, there are the three [roots] beginning with *uṣmagata*; for a female or a male, two are obtained; the same applies to the fourth;
for a female, she obtains two kinds as before—namely, the female root of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and the male root of goodness—because if the female form transforms into a male, she obtains it;
whereas for a male, in the case of the fourth root of goodness, he obtains only one, namely the male [root]. (Note: This passage cites the formal argument from the treatise.)

One attains only the roots of goodness of a male and does not attain those of a female; this is simply because having already attained a female body is not a state of definitive discernment (*niścaya*).
The abandonment by a noble one (*ārya*) occurs through the loss of the stage (*bhūmi*), while the abandonment by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) occurs through death;

this clarifies the meaning of "abandonment. As for the noble one’s abandonment of the four roots of goodness, such as *uṣmagata*, it is through the loss of the stage—that is, the abandonment of that specific stage.
If the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) migrate to a higher stage, they then incur a loss; at the time this stage is lost, the roots of goodness are finally relinquished.
However, if one dies in this stage and is reborn in this same stage, the stage is not lost; therefore, the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and other factors are not relinquished.

If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) relinquishes them, it is because an ordinary person lacks the provisions for the path of vision (*darśanamārga*); thus, they are relinquished at the end of life. (The above is the main text from the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*). Now, I shall further cite the *Vibhāṣā*.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* explains this, stating: "Once one has attained *kṣānti*, one departs from the evil destinies (*apāya*);

those such as *ṣaṇḍha* (eunuchs) and others have bodies that are contemptible, and they are the 'evil destinies' among humans. Since one who has attained the superior roots of goodness such as *kṣānti* will certainly not again receive a body of that kind, [it follows that] when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has attained *kṣānti* reaches the end of life, they relinquish their *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous character)."

Is patience (*kṣānti*) also abandoned? If it were so, what would be the fault? If it were abandoned, one would fall into the evil destinies; yet it is said that one does not fall into the evil destinies.
Furthermore, if it were abandoned, why is it that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) abandon [patience] at the time of death while noble ones (*ārya*) do not?
If it is not abandoned, why are both the "aggregate of karma" (*karmaskandha*) and the "sixfold aggregate" (*ṣaḍvidhaskandha*) not mentioned together, as is said regarding ordinary beings?
Regarding the question of whether one who is born or dwelling in the womb, etc., accomplishes bodily karma, the answer should be stated as follows: "One abandons [it]," and so forth.
An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), upon death, necessarily abandons the roots of goodness of patience because their faculties are inferior.

Since an ordinary person relies on this stage to give rise to these types of roots of goodness, if they die and are reborn in this same stage, they abandon them because they have abandoned their homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*). This is certainly the case for the higher stages; how much more so for this one?
The roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) are dharmas of the form realm (rūpadhātu) that, having arisen in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), shall not be abandoned.
"Heat" (uṣmagata) necessarily leads to nirvāṇa. [Note:

Regarding the initial stages, there are also distinctions among the various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*): that which corresponds to the stage of "hearing" (*śruta*) is called "foremost" (*agra*); that which corresponds to the stage of "reflection" (*cintā*) is called "superior" (*viśiṣṭa*);

that which corresponds to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) is called "long" (*dīrgha*); that which corresponds to "heat" (*uṣmagata*) is called "venerable" (*guruka*); that which corresponds to the "summit" (*mūrdhan*) is called "exalted" (*uttama*);

that which corresponds to "patience" (*kṣānti*) is called "sublime" (*praṇīta*); and that which corresponds to the subsequent [stage] is the same as the *Xuanwen*. Furthermore, the treatise states: "When this reaches the limit of the summit, it is called 'foremost'."

Because it is subsumed within the superior grade, it is called "Exalted"; because it is auspicious, it is called "Prosperity"; because it is the essence of growth, it is called "Long Body"; because this diligence is honored, it is called "Noble Nature";

because it is firm and stable, it is called "Supreme Fulfillment"; because it fulfills all aspirations, it is called "Wondrous"; furthermore, because it acts as the immediate condition for the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), it is called "Most Transcendent";
and because it surpasses all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is called "Victorious" and "Surpassing All Worlds."

The mundane roots of goodness are called "long" because they are able to reach superior virtues; they are called "venerable" because they are non-dual; they are called "superior" because they resemble the untainted (*anāsrava*); and they are called "sublime" for the same reason.

Furthermore, they are called "long" because they are the final mind of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*); they are called "supreme" because they are most capable of opening the gateway to the Noble Path;
and they are called "sharp" because their faculties are keen. They are the most excellent among all the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Therefore, it is called "Venerable" (*bhadanta*); because it subdues all enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called "Supreme";
because it draws forth the fruits of love, it is called "Sublime.

As cited from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it says: "When the various afflictions of the lower stages have not yet been severed at the causal stage, upon reaching the foot of the tree, by means of the nine [uninterrupted paths]..."

The nine unimpeded knowledges (*anantarya-jñāna*) and the nine liberations (*vimokṣa*) together constitute eighteen; the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) together constitute sixteen.

These thirty-four moments of mind represent the meaning of simultaneous abandonment (*sakṛt-prahāṇa*) according to the *Abhidharmakośa*. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "The afflictions of the lower eight stages have already been abandoned at the time of first practicing dhyāna;

only the nine grades of the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) remain in their entirety" (and so forth). This is the view of the *Abhidharmakośa* and Nāgārjuna.
In both cases, there should be no error regarding the grasping of the abandonment. When practicing dhyāna, the afflictions have already been severed and are not severed again;

however, according to other schools cited in the *Jñānaprasthāna*, although they are severed by means of contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava*), this is not yet termed "severance. It is only when one reaches the foot of the tree that the eight stages, including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), are all simultaneously severed, and thus they can all be termed "untainted" (*anāsrava*).

The fifth commentary on the *Zhiguan* (Stopping and Contemplation) records that this is merely the passage concerning the refutation of the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva*) within each of the four *siddhāntas* among the objects for converting others.

As for the refutation of nature within the world-realm (*loka-siddhānta*), it says: "Or it is taught that the mind contains all dharmas, as in the saying: 'The triple world has no distinction [from the mind].'"
The Dharma is solely created by the one mind; or it is said that all phenomena arise through conditions, as in the saying:

"A spiritual friend is a great causal condition," meaning they provide guidance and transformation; or it is said that all phenomena arise from the co-arising of causes and conditions, as in the saying:
"Mercury mixed with pure gold can coat various forms and images"; or it is said that all phenomena arise apart [from these], as in... [the saying].
It is said that the twelve links of dependent origination were not created by the Buddha, for their nature is such of itself; the same applies to the refutations of the other three *siddhāntas*.
It concerns only the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*) and so forth, which are desirable within the six realms of existence.

Among the six realms of existence, take for instance the three miserable paths (trāya), which manifest suffering as their characteristic, have retribution for evil deeds as their nature, and consist in the crushing of both form and mind as their substance;
their power lies in climbing onto blades and entering cauldrons—all of these are simply suffering. Could they also be called "lovable"?

What is here termed "lovable" refers merely to the craving for the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), which can summon the fruits of the three miserable paths; it is within those fruits that [the term] is spoken of.

For this reason, it is said to be "lovable. As for what is called "hateful," it refers to the loathing of the five sense objects that gives rise to a mind of anger, which likewise invites evil results;
this, too, is merely speaking of the cause within the context of the result.
Therefore, it is excluded that there are universal teachings without partiality or truths; because these are provisional, they do not exist.

these aspects of inclusion are as follows: within the twelve links of dependent origination, *saṃskāra* (volitional formations) and *bhava* (existence) encompass their nature; ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) encompass their essence;

Within each [element], one may open up four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
if one says that earth exists, this "existence" is the real, and "real" has the meaning of solidity; if one says that earth does not exist, this too is...

even to say that water is neither existent nor non-existent is likewise to say it abides. Now, there are four phrases regarding non-abiding, yet it is also not...

fire does not arise from itself, nor does it arise without a cause. Because it is fundamentally without self-nature and exists only by depending on conditions, it is called unreal.
Since the observation of form is thus, each of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness enters the limit of reality (*yathābhūta*).
In the two phrases, "encountering a spiritual friend" and "receiving instruction according to the Dharma," there is the character "difficult" (難) following each.
This is the fire of liberation through inexhaustible transformation and understanding.
The character "turn" (zhuǎn) is an error; it should be "wheel" (lún). That sūtra states:
A brāhmaṇa said to Sudhana, "Good son, I have only attained this bodhisattva liberation of the inexhaustible wheel (*akṣayacakra*).
Like the great flames of merit of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, it can burn away all the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of all sentient beings so that none remain, ensuring they never regress."

"How could I possibly know or explain this? Furthermore, by practicing and studying writing and calculation, one immediately attains entry into the dharma-gates of all arts, supernatural powers, and wisdom (and so forth).
[Note: In the sutra text below the section on the dharma of seals, the character 'gate' (門) is absent. "
One hundred lakṣas and ten thousand make ten thousand; one hundred thousand makes one lakṣa.
[This refers to] the internal and external grains.
The Sūtra describes these as the internal granules.
It states that one knows the number of sentient beings up to the number of the Tathāgata’s names;
the Sūtra says: "One can know the number of sentient beings, one can know the number of the categories of all dharmas, and one can know the distinctions among all dharmas."
The "separate enumeration" is able to know the enumeration of all three periods of time; it is able to know the enumeration of the names of all sentient beings;
it is able to know the enumeration of the names of all dharmas; and it is able to know the enumeration of the names of all Tathāgatas, and so forth.
[In the sutra text, the word "dharma" is omitted below.]
"Yan" (pronounced yàn) refers to a black mole on the face.
It is used to signify the contemplation of the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*).

Increasing the number up to ten and aligning it with the multiplication by ten does not necessarily mean that from the third increase onward, it is entirely identical to the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), the breaking of pervasiveness (*paryanta-bheda*), and so forth.
The meaning is this: one cultivates two dharmas and then enters the increased cultivation of three dharmas;

having cultivated three, one does not enter the increased cultivation of four dharmas, and so on, proceeding from the few to the many. Therefore, it is said that from beginning to end there is no fixed [limit], yet the number ten is used for the sake of comparison.

The ten vehicles of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* differ in name but are identical in meaning; to claim they are the same based on mere conjecture is to force a uniformity. Furthermore, from the fourth to the eighth vehicle are merely the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
Other practices are those that bring benefit through their respective gates, serving as the beginning and end [of the path].

As with the three dharmas, there are three aspects for each of hearing, reflection, and cultivation—namely, the essence of the three wisdoms, the practice of the three wisdoms, the fruit of the three wisdoms, and the function of the three wisdoms;
other practices may be understood by analogy with these explanations.
In the first section, if one discusses it from beginning to end, it must likewise comprise ten elements:
starting with the inconceivable realm and ending with the departure from attachment to dharmas;
this explains the meaning of "binding the conditions."
The text states: "Binding the object of focus is *śamatha*; a single thought-moment is *vipaśyanā*.

The first character of the initial "four foundations of mindfulness" (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) is erroneous; it should read "by means of the four foundations of mindfulness" (*caturbhiḥ smṛtyupasthānaiḥ*).
Regarding the formation of the "neither-nor" [position], the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "The ultimate non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena is the meaning of impermanence.

This refers to the Tripiṭaka masters' clarification that the impermanence of coarse and subtle arising and ceasing is the meaning of impermanence, not the meaning of non-impermanence. If one realizes that all phenomena are...

Because one falsely conceptualizes arising and ceasing where there is neither arising nor ceasing, when one examines arising through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), it cannot be found; thus, there is no cessation.

This state of neither-arising-nor-ceasing is the meaning of impermanence (*anityatā*). As for the meaning of suffering (*duḥkha*) being the thorough penetration of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as empty and non-arising:

the Tripiṭaka school elucidates the coarse and subtle five aggregates as the meaning of "this is suffering" and "this is not suffering," whereas the Mahāyāna school elucidates them from the perspective of the Vaipulya gate.

To realize that, by nature, there is no coarse or subtle suffering because it arises from false perception, and to see that what exists is itself emptiness such that the characteristic of suffering is not perceived—this is called "non-arising," which is the meaning of suffering.
That all phenomena are ultimately non-existent is the meaning of emptiness;

this is the emptiness of both persons and phenomena as elucidated by the Tripiṭaka masters. This is merely the practice of realizing emptiness within the path, not the ultimate meaning of emptiness itself.
These dharmas are precisely the true suchness (tathatā) and the real mark of emptiness; they have originally no self (*ātman*) nor non-self (*anātman*).
Because one falsely discriminates that they exist, one speaks of "non-self. If one does not apprehend a self, there is likewise no non-self. Self and non-self are originally non-dual.
That which is non-dual is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). The very nature of the absence of intrinsic nature is the meaning of true non-self.
Furthermore, the Dharma is fundamentally unborn and thus now without cessation; this state of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) is what is elucidated in the Tripiṭaka.
To return from existence to non-existence is termed "quiescent extinction," but this is merely a state of quiescence, not the true meaning of quiescent extinction.
The Mahāyāna school clarifies that all phenomena have, from the very beginning, been characterized by constant and inherent quiescence; this is Great Nirvāṇa, which cannot be further extinguished.

This is the meaning of true cessation (*bhūta-nirodha*). It continues until it says: "The general explanation of the five meanings within the Mahāyāna may also be taken as the five meanings of the Perfect [Teaching].
The ten objects, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, exist only within the three vehicles."

Upon seeing this passage, people immediately claim that the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) does not establish the realm of the *skandhas* (aggregates). Their intention is to say: "Since principle is pure and undefiled, how could there be any *skandhas*?
Consequently, they have made many such arbitrary assertions. Now, examining this text in detail, it is merely an exposition of the meaning of "opening up the provisional" (*kaiquan*).

It points out that the *skandhas* which are not yet identical [to reality] in the three previous teachings are, in the Perfect Teaching, identical in nature to the *skandhas*, coexisting within a single thought-moment as the essence of the body.
This is precisely the contemplative object for the initial mind of a person of the Perfect Teaching; I shall now cite the text to explain its meaning and pose a question regarding it.
For instance, as discussed in the *Yingluo Jing* (Sutra of the Necklaces), there are Buddha-lands that exclusively expound the Perfect Teaching without even the names of the three other teachings.

If such a land exclusively expounds the Perfect, how can a person at the initial stage of the Perfect Teaching set forth their practice when they lack the objective realm of the five aggregates (*skandhas*)? How do they begin?
Is it by contemplating the mind? Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the dharma-nature of the five aggregates is explained:
as for "form is the Buddha-nature," this is because the thirty-two marks and the Tathāgata’s eternal body are constant and never undergo change; therefore, form is said to be named the Buddha-nature.
As for "feeling is the Buddha-nature," this refers to the true bliss of the Tathāgata, namely, ultimate feeling in the sense of the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
If one holds that sensation is the eternal sensation of the Tathāgata and that perception is the Buddha-nature, then the true perception of the Tathāgata is called "perception of non-perception.
This "perception of non-perception" is not the perception of sentient beings as male or female; it is the eternal perception of the Tathāgata.

If one holds that volition is the Buddha-nature, then "volition" refers to the volition of longevity; by means of these causal conditions, one attains the eternally abiding longevity of the Tathāgata.
That consciousness is the Buddha-nature is precisely the Tathāgata’s mind of equality. Furthermore, it is said that by the extinction of this form, one attains eternal form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. That the five aggregates are eternally abiding is recorded without exception in all Mahāyāna sūtras.
Moreover, in the present *Xuánwén* (Mysterious Text), within the exposition of the three truths, the initial section on the conventional truth (*sāṃvṛti-satya*) cites the *Mahā-*.

The *Fenbie pin* (Chapter on Distinguishing) states: "Sentient beings have form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness," and further states: "Incomparable form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. The Record Master says:

"The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are themselves the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Since the aggregates reach the Buddha, one should know that the conventional truth also extends to the Buddha.
If one says there are no aggregates in perfect [enlightenment], it would mean that the ultimate and middle truths lack the conventional truth. It also states: "The preceding three..."

In the teachings for those of initial resolve, the cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) means that at the stage of initial resolve, one aggregate is all aggregates—this refers to the emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle of the five aggregates of the hundred realms.
Furthermore, the *Wenju ji* (Commentary on the Text) also states: "The initial resolve of the two teachings both involves the cessation of the aggregates;

the initial resolve of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) likewise merely breaks through the aggregates, whereas only the Perfect [Teaching] contemplates the three thousand [realms] within a single thought-moment."
The perfection of the Truths (satya) is precisely the One Mind containing all minds, the One Body containing all bodies, and the One Land containing all lands.

Since it speaks of body and mind, how could the aggregates (skandha) be absent? Furthermore, since it speaks of the Three Thousand Worlds as the perfection of the Three Truths, if one were not to establish the aggregates, one would only be discussing two thousand worlds.
The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) states: "The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) consists of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

One should understand that this true body of real wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) also possesses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); the causes and conditions for its response and transformation likewise possess the five aggregates;
and the principle of the inherent virtue of sentient beings also possesses the five aggregates. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "A bodhisattva should not form the thought:
'I shall, by means of true wisdom, cause all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) to be purified and dwell within them. Why is this?"
Therefore, dharmas have no place of abiding. Just as earth rests upon water, water rests upon wind, and wind rests upon space, space has nothing upon which it rests;
fundamentally, there is no such thing as abiding. That which precedes the limit is saṃsāra, and that which follows the limit is nirvāṇa;

both are unobtainable, for this is the absence of the aggregates (skandhas). Conventional truth is the phenomenon. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "All dharmas tend toward form"—this is their tendency.
However, as for the fact that form (*rūpa*) is largely the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is because the three truths of the aggregates (*skandha*) are fundamentally one;

being identical in essence whether existent or non-existent, they are termed "nature-aggregate" (*svabhāva-skandha*). This nature-aggregate is inconceivable, for it is due to sentient beings' delusion regarding this nature-aggregate that the "phenomenal aggregate" (*vastu-skandha*) arises.
Therefore, within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one is led to contemplate the phenomenal aggregate so as to manifest the nature-aggregate, thereby destroying the defiled aggregate.

Because he dwells within the aggregates (*skandhas*) of the true reality (*dharmatā*), it is said that the Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body and so forth are such; how could an unworthy person like myself dare to speak in opposition?
For the true principle of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings is like the moon beyond the clouds—it does not speak of the existence of aggregates.

The Separate Teaching (*Pratyekabuddha-yāna*) speaks of the Middle Principle, which does not possess aggregates, yet the principle exists outside the aggregates; only after the aggregates of the nine realms have been destroyed can it be attained.
If this is so, it is clear that the three preceding teachings do not establish the aggregates (skandhas), whereas the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) establishes them; this is now made manifest.
I address those of later talent: who among you will reflect upon this? Do not claim that the Perfect Teaching lacks the aggregates as its doctrinal principle.
Regarding the preceding four [categories],
their circularity is determined by the text on the shallow and deep levels according to the four teachings; therefore,
they are separately distinguished once again.
It should be stated as "discriminating.
The fundamental [teaching] first destroys [the notion of permanence] by designating the four frontiers.
"Great falsehood comes first" explains the fundamental delusion;

that is, claiming "I have attained the qualities of a superior person," "I have entered noble wisdom," or "I have attained the noble dharmas," and so forth—referring to the fourfold divisions found in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations)—from the stage of impurity-contemplation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) up to the four fruits of the path. To say "I have attained these" constitutes [the first great falsehood].

To have committed a grave offense and yet claim to possess faith, precepts, generosity, learning, wisdom, eloquence, the untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*), the two types of emptiness-wisdom (*śūnyatā-jñāna*) regarding phenomena and persons, the arrival of devas, nāgas, and spirits to make offerings, or the attainment of the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*)—all such claims constitute violations.
In this present age, those who lack the eye of instruction and are shrouded in darkness all style themselves as "enlightened"; this is truly a great falsehood.

This is the precept against stealing from the Three Jewels interchangeably. Stealing money in an amount reaching five *māṣakas* constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). The objects of theft are manifold;

furthermore, regarding the phrase "interchangeably" in relation to the Three Jewels, there are two types: first, interchange between the Three Jewels; second, interchange within their respective portions. "Interchange" refers to when an administrator takes [property]...
If one takes the monastic community’s provisions, utensils, oxen, or horses to serve as offerings for a Buddha image, it constitutes a grave offense;
the same applies to using property belonging to the Buddha or the Dharma for the personal use of the monastic community.

Even if there is only a single coin of property belonging to a Buddhist stūpa, because it was surrendered by a donor with a sincere heart, gods and humans should conceive the notion of "Buddha" and the notion of "stūpa" regarding that object, even down to a blade of grass.
If rain blows upon them and they become rotten, one must not use them for offerings to the Tathāgata’s stūpa, as no one would assign a price to such items.
Furthermore, the Vinaya states that even feathers falling from a Buddha hall or a stūpa must not be used, because all devas perceive them as being the Buddha.
Regarding "changing the substance" (tǐ-hù): this refers to cases where an original image of Śākyamuni is altered to become Amitābha, or an original [image]... [is changed].
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the term for "nirvāṇa" was altered to "monastic quarters," and those intended for monastic housing were converted into vehicles;
while these changes may seem reasonable from the perspective of their practical application toward external objects, they violate the donor's intention and thus incur the offense of misappropriation.

Today, many religious leaders forcibly seize the food, drink, rice, and flour belonging to the monastery, or take the funds for incense, oil, candles, and lamps from the halls, using them for their own private benefit.
Although its use may provide sustenance for the body for a single day, it will cause one to fall into suffering for a thousand kalpas;
would those with discernment not feel a chill of horror upon seeing this?
It is a poor matchmaker indeed.

This is the precept against matchmaking. To convey a man’s intent to a woman, or a woman’s intent to a man, and thereby facilitate a marriage or a private liaison, constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension).

According to the Vinaya texts, the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is incurred only when three stages are complete: first, receiving the message; second, going to deliver it; and third, returning to report the result.

If two stages are complete, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense); if only one stage is complete, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* further recommends that the matchmaker encourage the parties to return to their respective homes.

If a wife returns early, one commits an offense of *thullaccaya* (*āna*). It is also said that if one seeks out fine stallions for another and facilitates their mating, one likewise commits an offense of *thullaccaya*.
[End of] Chapter on the Dwelling.
There are two types of precepts regarding rooms: first, the precept concerning a room without an owner that exceeds the prescribed measure without the consent of the Saṃgha;

second, the precept concerning a room with an owner that is built without the consent of the Saṃgha. Regarding the precept on rooms without an owner, there are five reasons: first, it requires manpower for its management, which hinders one's progress in the path of cultivation;
second, as the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states, it increases one's own bonds of greed and destroys the virtues of few desires and contentment.
Third, by begging and seeking in various places, one troubles and disturbs both humans and non-humans;

because they do not develop faith or respect, this causes the True Dharma to be destroyed and prevents it from remaining for long. Fourth, by acting solely according to one's own will and not soliciting instructions, one permits obstacles to monastic affairs and causes much disturbance.
Fifth, by violating the precepts and harming one’s own conduct, one contravenes the path of compassion and ruins the pure life (brahmacarya). Sixth, the conditions...

The conditions for committing this offense are six: first, it must be without an owner; second, it must be for one's own sake; third, one must have personally requested the materials; fourth, it must exceed the prescribed dimensions and not have been formally authorized;
fifth, one must perceive it as exceeding the dimensions and not having been authorized; sixth, once the dwelling is completed, one incurs the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (residual) offense.

Regarding the gravity of the offense, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that the length should be twelve *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha’s hand and the width seven *vitasti*. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, a *vitasti* of the Buddha’s hand is equivalent to two Chinese feet.
If that is so, "difficult places" (*durgama*) refer to locations measuring two zhang and four chi in width and one zhang and four chi in length where there are tigers, wolves, or ants;
furthermore, crossroads where many people gather for games, brothels, market stalls, and places where wild beasts are pastured are all difficult places.
Regarding "obstructed places" (*āvṛta*), the Vinaya states: "To the extent that even a grass cart cannot pass through."

Regarding "turning back" (reversal): furthermore, human fields and gardens, as well as official lands, the grounds of lay devotees (*gṛhapati*), non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and *bhikṣuṇīs*, are all obstructed sites.
As for the precept concerning rooms with owners, the Vinaya states: "If this room belongs to one's own person, and they die, go far away, or do not return, one may dispose of it as one pleases;
however, if it belongs to the Three Jewels, to relatives, or to laypeople (*avadātavasana*), one must sell it oneself and take the money."
To act with mastery according to one's mind, one must simply refrain from selling land; as the record says, "Welcome the good," and the current commentator wishes for people to do good.
An (Dao'an) questioned [the propriety of] clothing.
The three robes and one alms bowl are the insignia of entering the Path. The robes must be of the proper dimensions and dyed in blue-black or madder-brown;

only after they meet these requirements for size and color may the ritual procedures for consecration and the recitation of protective mantras be performed. Otherwise, one will remain without robes for a lifetime;
if one accepts the faithful offerings of others under such conditions, one falls into the transgression of misappropriating such gifts.

The *Baoxu* (寶疏) states that an alms bowl should be made of iron or ceramic and should be of the proper measure; after it has been fumigated, one should perform the ritual of adding mantras and receiving it for use.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says that to keep a wooden bowl constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that keeping a wooden bowl is a mark of non-Buddhists; therefore, from a doctrinal standpoint, it must be [avoided].
He criticized them at Nanshan, saying: "Those who claim to study the Mahāyāna do not even know the impropriety of acting as matchmakers for brothels;
how much less could they possibly understand the bowl and robe, or the proper manner of receiving food?"
Regarding items for sustaining the body, one must receive them only when they are beneficial; otherwise, one incurs an offense.

The Vinaya establishes many rules, yet one primary intent behind these regulations is to prevent theft. Second, the recipient must be a fully ordained *bhikṣu* who maintains the precepts with purity and without violation.
Third, as for the object of the transaction, the *bhikṣu* may not take food for himself; if there is no [other recipient], [the rule applies].
The *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) heats the vessel himself and places it down; the *kappiya-kāraka* pours in the rice, and [the monk] cooks it himself.

Once it is cooked, he receives it from another, following the six methods for receiving food. Among the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya], three additional methods of receiving are added. To state the essentials briefly:
in all cases of eating roasted flour, cakes, soup, fruit, or any other edible food, one must receive it from a *kappiya-kāraka*, even if it is snow.

In places where there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), it is permitted to take hail for one's own consumption; if one exists, one should receive it from them. Otherwise, one commits the offense of theft.

Nowadays, many practitioners of meditation increase their food intake, claiming it is "cultivating merit" (*puṇya*), yet they do not realize they are committing the offense of eating what is unwholesome to touch (*duṭṭhullāpatti*).

Furthermore, they cause those who receive the food to fall into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) and incur various evil retributions. This is because they have never studied or learned the teachings and are thus deluded regarding the Dharma.
Furthermore,
there are four kinds of medicinal substances: first, timely medicines (*kālabhaiṣajya*), which refer to parched flour, cooked rice, dry rice, flowers, fruits, and fine powders for grinding into food.
Lotus root, radish, rice gruel, and curd may be consumed from dawn until midday; these are permitted by the Holy Teaching.
Second, non-timely medicines (*akālabhaiṣajya*) refer to ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, and fresh fruit juice, which must be purified with water before being permitted for drinking.

Third, seven-day medicines (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*) refer to molasses syrup, raw butter, refined butter, and the five kinds of animal fats; those who receive them are permitted to purify them with water.
There are four types of medicines permitted to be consumed for the duration of one's life (*yāvajjīva-bhaiṣajya*): namely, black pepper (*marica*), *viśālā*, and *harītakī*.
These medicines are not fit to serve as food and are thus termed "life-long medicines. It is permitted to take them over a long period so that they may effectively eliminate ailments.

There are three kinds of "lifespans" (*ākṛti*): first, the lifespan of the medicine; second, the lifespan of the disease; and third, the lifespan of karmic retribution (*vipāka*). All the aforementioned medicines must be obtained from a pure source.

Having received [the medicine] from another person, one may consume it only after performing the formal rite of adding the *prātimokṣa* (confession) formula; however, this requirement for adding the formula does not apply to *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines to be taken at specific times).
The method of receiving [the medicine] is as prescribed in the Vinaya. One should sit in seclusion.

The precept regarding sitting with a woman in a secluded place refers to a location where sexual intercourse could take place. According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, if the door is closed and no one is present, the offense is a *pāyattika* (falling);

if someone is outside the door, it is a *duṣkṛta* (misdeed). Even if she is one's own sister, a lay attendant (*upāsaka*), or someone who is asleep, insane, or an infant—if one sits with such a person in a secluded place, it is likewise termed an offense.

Regarding the precept on sitting in the open with a woman: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one sits in an open space with a woman, for every time one rises and then sits again, one incurs a *pācittiya* offense.
If, while sitting, one remains at a distance of one *vyāma* (fathom), one incurs a *pācittiya*; at one and a half *vyāmas*, it is a *dukkaṭa*; at two *vyāmas*, there is no offense.

Does preaching the Dharma for men or women constitute a transgression of the precept against exceeding limits? The Vinaya states: "If one is not requested to speak, it is permitted to speak no more than five or six words;
if one is requested to preach, or if asked about the meaning, one may speak as much as required. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, by means of these five or six words, one attains [the merit].

The *Jieben zhijie* (Explanation of the Formulation of Precepts) in the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) states: "The five phrases refer to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness being without self (*anātman*).
The six phrases refer to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind being impermanent (*anitya*). Regarding the preaching of the Dharma to women, it requires the presence of a man;
this must be a wise man who understands human affairs and can serve as a witness—specifically, a layman—and not one who seeks [personal gain].
Regarding the witness of another woman: the woman’s state of desire is the same [as the monk’s].
This refers to the precept on sleeping in the same room as a woman; it concerns a bhikṣu sleeping in the same room as a woman, whether the woman arrives later or [the monk arrives first].
If a bhikṣu arrives later, or if two arrive together, or if she lies down on her side and turns over from side to side, he commits a *thullaccaya* for each instance.
This applies even with a mother, an animal, a human, a eunuch, or a person with both sexual organs. Furthermore, if a bhikṣu lies down during the day while a woman stands, he also commits an offense.
This concerns the precept against traveling in the same boat as a bhikṣuṇī. Traveling in the same boat with a laywoman also constitutes an offense;
however, according to the Vinaya, there is no offense in cases of crossing directly across [a river], when using a boatman’s vessel for the sake of safety, or when traveling up or down a stream.
[Xuanzang’s Translation]:

*Thūlaccaya* is translated here as "Great Obstruction" (*dà zhàng*), meaning that one who commits it can obstruct the path to wholesome rebirths; this is the preliminary stage (*upāya*) for violating the precepts.
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states: "This is the preliminary stage for a grave offense. In the Vinaya, it is sometimes placed after the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṅghādisesa), because...

The offenses subsumed under the category of *śīla* (precepts) are grave, such as those involving the preparatory stages (*prayoga*)—both distant and proximate—of the first two categories, as well as the principal offenses (*maula-āpatti*) of schism in the Sangha and stealing four *māṣaka* coins, and so forth.
Those below the level of *pratideśanīya* are subsumed under *airyāpathika* (proper deportment) and are termed light.

In the Vinaya, there are many meanings for the term *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), which are not uniform; they refer to the gravity of cause and effect, as well as independent (*svatantra*) offenses.
As for the nature of these [offenses]: when one first gives rise to the thought with the intent to approach a sexual object, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).
When body and mind proceed toward the act, one incurs a light *sthūlātyaya*. Upon reaching the object and making physical contact, one incurs a heavy *sthūlātyaya*.

This applies to all preliminary stages (*pūrvaprayoga*) of the other three *pārājika* offenses as well. If the act is completed, one incurs a *pārājika* offense. Furthermore, if one subsequently gives rise to a mind of rejoicing or gratification, that too constitutes an offense.

The second section on minor offenses (*dukkaṭa*) consists of two types of preparatory acts (*paccaya-kamma*): light *dukkaṭa* and heavy *dukkaṭa*. The term *phala-lan* (fruit-offense) is also called *ekato-mūla* (independent offense);
it refers to using human skin, a stone alms-bowl, or pouring [liquids] into the lower part [of the body]. As for the *hetu-lan* (cause-offense), it refers to the preliminary act of sexual misconduct.
A light *lan* refers to tearing one's three robes out of anger; a heavy *lan* refers to causing a schism in the Saṃgha and so forth. Now, it says:

Regarding the aforementioned associates, it is said that for the offenses of causing a schism in the Saṃgha, stealing four *kārsāpaṇas*, or stealing food belonging to the Saṃgha—specifically referring to property designated as permanently held for the ten directions (*daśadig-satata-sthiti*) or property currently present before the deceased members of the fivefold assembly (*pañca-varga*) provided it does not constitute the full measure of five coins—as well as sexual misconduct with improper objects and theft, these are categorized into three grades. Among them, the superior grade is as follows: [text continues].
Non-humans and the like are all subsumed under the upper grade. As for the middle grade:

for example, causing a schism in the Saṃgha through formal ritual (karmavācanā), stealing three coins, or creating the conditions for a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. Regarding the conditions for a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense:

emitting semen for another, touching a person of both sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana) or a eunuch (paṇḍaka), or touching hair and nails [of such persons], and so forth—all these are subsumed under the middle grade. As for the lower grade: reviling with an evil mind.
A monk stole one coin, used human hair, ate raw meat, and shaved the hair from three places;
"three places" refers to the armpits and the passages for both excrement and urine. Furthermore, he poured ghee and honey down the lower part—that is, the lower orifice.

Furthermore, those who keep stone alms bowls, practice naked asceticism, wear the garments of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), wear bird feathers, wear skins, or subsist on wind and air—all such practices belong to the category of the inferior.
According to the *Maudgalyāyana-questions-on-retribution-sūtra*, committing even one offense of *sthūlātyaya* leads to falling into hell; when asked for the number of years [spent there], it is five.
One hundred and sixty million [years].
From the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (舍墮) downward, as well as those prescribed in various sūtras, are all termed "residual" (*śeṣa*).
In the Sanskrit language, *niḥsargika-pāyattika* is translated here as "abandonment and forfeiture" (*she-duo*). Following this, from the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (僧殘) onward...
The *Xià* (Lower) commentary refers to those [rules] following the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* as "subsequent retinue" (*hòu juànshǔ*), while those not derived from the Vinaya are termed "remainder" (*yú*).
The *Xuán* (Profound) commentary offers two different explanations regarding whether these are included or excluded;

it differs from the *Xià* in that it considers everything from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* downward as "subsequent retinue," whereas the *Xià* considers everything from the *naiḥsargika-pāyantikā* downward as "subsequent retinue. This constitutes one point of disagreement between the two.
Furthermore, the *Xuán* [Commentary] uses the twenty-four precepts as "remainder" (*yú*), while the *Qiān* [Commentary] uses those from the *pāyattika* downward as "remainder.

This may be because the author feared that the compiler of the record might consider the *pāyattika* to be the remainder of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or it may be a textual error; let scholars examine this carefully.
[Xuán] The Fangdeng Ershisi Jiejing states:
"If a bodhisattva sees a starving sentient being come seeking food and drink and does not give it, they violate the first precept.
If they engage in unrestrained sexual desire, choosing even among birds and beasts, they violate the second precept. [Seeing a fellow...]
To maintain a wife and children while speaking of their faults constitutes the third precept; to see someone in sorrow or distress and further increase their anger constitutes the fourth precept;
to encounter wealth on a deserted road and take it immediately constitutes the fifth precept;
as for the remaining precepts... (and so forth).

Regarding the statement that one obtains the precepts of the True Dharma through the side of "receiving": since these are fundamentally obtained through "arousing" [the aspiration], the current mention of "receiving" may be due to the fact that they are aroused by means of receiving,
or it may be an error.

Regarding "not [dwelling on] various evil thoughts," the *Nirvāṇa-śūtra* commentary states that one should be free from the eight evil thoughts: first, desire; second, ill-will; third, malice; fourth, thoughts of kinsmen; fifth, thoughts of the country;
sixth, thoughts of immortality; seventh, thoughts of contempt; and eighth, thoughts of lineage.
Regarding the eight worldly concerns—gain and loss, and so forth:
upon gaining profit one feels joy; upon encountering loss, distress; upon being reviled, anger; upon being praised, delight; upon receiving commendation, the mind becomes elated;
upon being ridiculed, resentment arises; upon meeting suffering, one harbors grief; and upon encountering pleasure, one gives rise to indulgence.
The Story of the Butcher Kāṭhika:
After King Ajātaśatru had taken his father’s life and ascended the throne, the butcher Kāṭhika came to him and said to the king, "There is no retribution for good or evil deeds.
How do I know this? I recall having been born as a human being for seven lifetimes."
"If there is such evil in the heavens that it brings about retribution, why was he born among humans and devas? Because of this doubt, he went to question the Buddha.

The Buddha said, "Because you made a perverse vow when you gave food to a pratyekabuddha in the past, saying, 'I shall always make the killing of oxen and sheep my profession,' you have been born seven times among humans and seven times in the heavens."
The *Acalaprasthāna-sūtra* and other scriptures state that one is not moved by forms or sounds, does not fall into the three evil realms, does not regress to the level of the two vehicles,
and is not shaken by the heterodox winds of divergent views.
[Xuanzang] This is called skillfully understanding the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, which states that all phenomena are neither produced nor abiding, not even for a single thought-moment;
they are like dreams and like mirages. One who knows this is said to uphold the discipline and is said to be skillfully understanding.
[Xuanzang] states: There should be a separate assembly of bodhisattvas;

once the provisional teachings have been opened, they become identical to the perfect [teachings], as in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, where there are no longer distinct Buddhas of the *Vaipulya* or *Āgama* vehicles, nor persons of the three vehicles—this is the fourth [point] concerning the distinction of the liberation precepts.
The minor offenses (duṣkṛta) are grouped together with the saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses;
they are so named because they appear at the end of the five categories of offenses. In Sanskrit, *duṣkṛta* means "badly done" (*akṛtya*).

The Vinaya divides these into two types: those pertaining to the body are called "badly done," while those pertaining to speech are called "badly spoken. What are the characteristics of these offenses?
This constitutes the preliminary application (*upāya*) for all the various precepts. Furthermore, there may still be errors; for instance, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct:

if one gives rise to the intention and desire to act but has not yet moved, it is a preliminary application. If one gives rise to an unwholesome mind with the intent to move body and speech, it is subsumed under "intentional action" (*saṃcetanīya*).

This applies even if the mind is not focused on right mindfulness, such as when speaking frivolous or false words out of playfulness, or even regarding robes, bowls, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions.

Whether urinating, sitting, lying down, speaking, or remaining silent, one should always maintain single-minded concentration; to act otherwise is an error. If one repents, the offense may be either light or heavy:
a heavy offense requires confession before another (*pratideśanīya*), while a light offense requires only mental remorse (*cittapratyavekṣā*).

Regarding the term *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it refers to the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. Concerning those who violate these precepts, the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "It is like a person acting for the sake of another..."
It is so named because, after being cut, a remnant of the throat remains. Regarding confession, there are four methods: first, the purification of the emotional transgression of concealment;
second, the purification of the offense of concealment; third, the purification of the emotional transgression of the remainder, which is the *ṣaḍrātra-mānatva* (six-night penance);

and fourth, the purification of the offense of the remainder, which is the removal of the offense by a community of twenty monks. These are all cases of *śeṣa-duṣkṛta* (remaining offenses) within the Vinaya.

This refers to the specific distinctions among the various methods of repentance (*chān-fǎ*). Now, you ask why it is said that they are all generally treated as "confession before another" (*duìshǒu*). How is this known?

The *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) mentions "mediating marriages," which is precisely the "sexual intercourse" mentioned in the *Fanwang jing* (Brahmajāla Sūtra). Furthermore, the *Sifen lü* mentions "slandering others based on false grounds," which is precisely the "groundlessly slandering virtuous people" mentioned in the *Fanwang jing*.
Moreover, the *Sifen lü* mentions "accepting the methods for destroying the Sangha," which is precisely the [corresponding] section in the *Fanwang jing*.

The net is torn; this refers to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) of the Saṃgha that turns the Wheel of Dharma. A sūtra states: "If one commits any of the forty-eight minor transgressions, by performing confession before another person (*pratideśanā*), the offense shall be extinguished.
One should know that within the Mahāyāna, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension from the community) are all subsumed under the category of minor stains."
The six types of barbarians sell liquor, speak of others' faults, praise themselves while disparaging others, are stingy, and slander the Triple Gem.
Śikṣamāṇā.
This is called the "female student of the Dharma" (*śikṣamāṇā*); she ranks below the fully ordained nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*) and above the novice nuns (*śrāmaṇerikā*).

Having trained her mind through the six rules, she may then receive the full nuns' precepts. These six rules are: intentional physical contact with a lustful mind, stealing four *māṣaka* coins or more, taking the life of an animal, speaking a minor falsehood, eating at improper times, and drinking alcohol.
The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states that there are eighteen types of young girls [who may become *śikṣamāṇās*].
It is said that one should study the precepts for two years; furthermore, it is stated that those who were married at a young age and were ten years old [may receive ordination].
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The two years are for training the body, and the six dharmas are for training the mind."
【Xuan】The *Mahā-śāstra on the Relish of Joy Arising in Each Stage* states:
"When one first attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the single-minded attachment to it is called 'relish' (*āsvāda*). Question:
All afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of causing deep attachment; why is only craving (*tṛṣṇā*) designated as "relish"? Answer: Craving resembles meditative concentration.
Why is this? Because in dhyāna, the mind is first gathered and firmly established; attachment is likewise focused and difficult to relinquish.
Consequently, the subsequent text states that "dhyāna" should be placed first.

This is fully contained within the "Chapter on Cultivation and Realization" (the seventh of the ten major chapters) of the Dhyāna-pāramitā, where the characteristics of cultivation and realization for each stage—
from the fundamental [dhyānas] up to the untainted (*anāsrava*)— are thoroughly distinguished.

【Xuanzang】 When the body is upright and the mind is collected, the breath becomes harmonious; one perceives that this mental path has become utterly clear and still, profoundly peaceful and secure, entering step by step.
If the mind remains fixed upon its object without wandering or scattering, this is called "coarse abiding" (sthūla-sthiti).
Following this state of mind, that which is more stable and superior to the preceding stage is called "subtle abiding" (*sūkṣma-vihāra*).
[Xuanzang’s Commentary: When the dharma of maintaining the body arises as subtle abiding, the body naturally becomes upright, free from fatigue or pain, as if supported by some external object.
Maintaining the power of the body.

[Xuanzang] In the desire realm, after the coarse and subtle abidings, for perhaps one or two days or one or two months, one gradually perceives a state that is deeper and more subtle; suddenly, the mind—
The earth appears as a single part, the body is clarified like a cloud or a shadow, and the mind is held by the power of concentration without distraction.

Although it is empty and pure, the marks of body and mind are still perceived; yet the various factors of merit have not yet fully developed—this is called the "concentration of the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*).
[Xuanzang] The eight tangibles refer to the eight:
movement, itching, lightness, heaviness, cold, warmth, roughness, and smoothness. These eight tangibles are the four great elements: movement and lightness are wind;
itching and warmth are fire; cold and smoothness are water; heaviness and roughness are earth.
[Emperor Xuan’s Commentary:

The six contemplations of the practice (*ṣaḍvidhābhāvanā*) discuss cause and effect together in twelve lines. First, regarding the fruit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it clarifies suffering (*duḥkha*), coarseness (*audārikatva*), and hindrance (*āvaraṇa*).
When a practitioner loathes the inferior matter and mind of the desire realm—being oppressed by hunger, thirst, cold, heat, knives, and staves—this body is termed "suffering."
The thirty-six impurities, such as excrement and urine, which are foul and filthy, are called "coarse. This body, being a material obstruction, is separated from mountains, rivers, stones, and walls;

this is called "obstructed. Next, regarding the fruit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*): because it clings to the superior, pure, and wondrous, and transcends the pleasures of the [Desire] Realm, it is called "superior.

Because it is like a reflection in a mirror, it is called "wondrous. Having attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), one is unimpeded by mountains or walls; this is called "transcending."
These are called the six fruits; there are further six causes, as fully detailed in the *Chanmen* (Dhyāna Gate).

[Xuánzàng’s Commentary: The eight noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), the four [remedies for] illness and so forth, and the four [contemplations on] impermanence—the first four of these are methods of remediation through the contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-darśana*), while the latter four are [remediations through the contemplation of principles].
Based on these conditions, one practices the contemplation of the truths through this method of observation, which has both general and specific aspects.

The general aspect refers to observing those four aggregates (*skandhas*) as a composite that lacks reality by means of eight contemplations. The specific aspect consists of the first four [contemplations] which serve to counteract the four aggregates:

viewing sensation (*vedanā*) as a disease, perception (*saṃjñā*) as an abscess, formations (*saṃskāra*) as a festering wound, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as a thorn; thus, one treats them with [the contemplations of] impermanence and so forth.

The contemplation of the four aggregates as impermanent, the contemplation of consciousness as suffering, the contemplation of sensation as empty, the contemplation of perception as non-self, and the contemplation of mental formations—

because these eight [contemplations] easily give rise to weary detachment, one cultivates them to attain the untainted (*anāsrava*). Since their names were not listed in the preceding profound text, they are set forth here.
To examine this by means of the four propositions is called "analytical deconstruction.
Regarding the third point, since it speaks of "observing and analyzing," one should ask:

does the movement and distraction of the mind occur because of two factors, or does it occur without being caused by two factors, or does it occur through a combination of both, or does it occur without cause? This is as explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mohe Zhiguan).

Within the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of this world, one should examine each of the four propositions: namely, whether the internal object of desire (*kāma-dhātu*) and the mental faculty (*manas*) are conjoined through self, other, or both, and so forth.
If one does not perform such examination but instead gives rise to birth according to the concentrations by practicing impure (*sāsrava*) dhyāna, the *Dhyāna-mukha* (Gate of Concentration) asks:
"The Bodhisattva path should explain the profound concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) which is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; why is this so?"
Regarding the statement that the four dhyānas of ordinary beings are worldly, outflowing, subject to birth and death, and deceptive phenomena—the answer is no.
The Bodhisattva knows that the five desires and the five hindrances arise from causes and conditions; they have no intrinsic nature, being empty and non-existent, and are thus very easy to abandon.
Sentient beings, however, are inverted in their views and become attached to these matters of desire; they crave meager and base pleasures while abandoning the dhyānas.
Because Bodhisattvas who dwell in the bliss of profound and wondrous meditative concentration give rise to a heart of compassion in order to deliver these sentient beings, they practice dhyāna,
depart from the five desires and the five hindrances, enter the first dhyāna, and successively enter the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; thus, by means of the methods of dhyāna,
they teach and transform sentient beings so as not to cause them to lose their Dharma-body or the life-force of wisdom.
[Master Xuanzang’s Translation] The fifth chapter, "The Gate of Dhyāna through Equanimity, Mindfulness, and Skillful Means," states:
Regarding the cultivation of the six practices, when one is in the sixth stage of silent mind within the first dhyāna, one develops revulsion toward applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
One regards the first dhyāna as inferior because one knows that these two factors agitate and afflict the concentrated mind.

One considers that the joy and bliss of concentration arising from vitarka and vicāra are coarse; these factors of vitarka and vicāra obstruct the internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) of the second dhyāna.
That which is called "obstructing" refers to the superior state above it. The internal purity of the second dhyāna is peaceful and thus called "superior.
Because it arises from internal purity, it is called "sublime. Having attained the second dhyāna, the mind achieves liberation; now, one wishes to distance oneself from this second dhyāna.
Based on three kinds of skillful means, one attains detachment: first, through neither accepting nor clinging; second, through censure;
and third, through analytical contemplation. This is explained in detail in the *Dhyanamukha*.

[Master Xuán] states in the ninth chapter, "Discriminating Between the Erroneous and the Correct in Calm Abiding and Insight": "If the mind takes sentient beings as its object and definitely perceives the thought of their attaining happiness, such that the mind is extremely clear,
yet one does not see sentient beings attaining happiness at the locus of the object, this is 'internal non-concealment while external concealment.'"
Alternatively, there may be cases where the internal mind is clear and pure while externally one sees sentient beings attaining happiness; this is "neither internally nor externally obscured.

As for those that are "obscured," they are erroneous; those that are "not obscured" are correct. Furthermore, the four immeasurables arising based on the fundamental dhyānas are with outflows (*sāsrava*);
those arising based on the [meditations on] impurity and so forth are without outflows (*anāsrava*). Those that are with outflows are erroneous; those that are without outflows are correct.

[Xuán]: Regarding the methods for both rejecting the lower and ascending to the upper, I shall now establish the first method of the sixth stage, the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), as an illustration. As for "rejecting the lower":

when a practitioner wishes to cultivate the concentration of the Sphere of Infinite Space, they must deeply contemplate the faults and transgressions of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). That is to say, if there is a physical body, then internally...
There are the sufferings of hunger, thirst, illness, and the need for excretion; there are the external sufferings of cold, heat, blades, staffs, and punishments.
Furthermore, all material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) bind the mind, depriving it of autonomy;

this is the prison of the mind that causes beings to experience affliction. This is a brief description of the characteristics of the faults of form. Those who aspire to higher realms praise empty space.
In the formless realm, these faults do not exist; this state is tranquil and free from all afflictions and calamities.
Therefore, what is clearly expressed as a reprimand is precisely the characteristic of practicing the contemplation of the six aspects.

[Xuanzang]: If one practices as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*), there are further distinct categories regarding the six subtle gates (*ṣaḍ-sūkṣma-dvārāṇi*), the special victories (*viśeṣa-mārga*), and the universal clarity (*samanta-prabhāsa*). Regarding the nature of wisdom (*prajñā-svabhāva*) and its degree, the *Dhyāna-gate* states:

"This is a teaching according to the capacities of beings (*yathā-bhavyatā-vinaya*). If one follows the application of antidotes, it is contrary to this [previous] explanation; the meaning is fully contained within the five preceding gates. Five gates.
It is my view that the fourfold afflictions are countered by meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), giving rise to the eighty-four thousand defilements (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, the five gates differ in their sequence and depth: first, the gate of breath-restraint (*ānāpāna*) is the mundane meditation of ordinary worldlings;
next, the gate of impurity (*aśubha*) is the supramundane meditation practiced by the Śrāvakas; next, the gate of loving-kindness (*maitrī*)...
