When the nose smells fragrances and discerns whether they are pleasant or unpleasant, it possesses the function of the eye; when beholding celestial palaces, the nose possesses the function of the eye. When reading scriptures or preaching the Dharma, one can discern them by smelling the fragrance; thus, the nose possesses the function of the ear.
When smelling the scents of the flowers, fruits, and seeds of various trees, as well as the aroma of ghee and oil, one can discern them;
thus, the nose possesses the function of the tongue. Furthermore, when one discerns lust, delusion, and anger by smelling their fragrance, [the nose likewise possesses the function of the mind].
The nose has intentional functions.
Regarding the ten kinds of six sense faculties,
for instance, in addition to the five eyes of the eye faculty, there are further the wisdom eye, the light-emitting eye, and the eye that transcends birth and death.
The unimpeded eye and the all-knowing eye constitute the tenth; the remaining faculties are likewise so.
The *Mahā-śāstra on the Transformation of the Indeterminate* asks: "If Śākyamuni transforms himself into immeasurable thousands of billions of Buddhas, how is it that he can do so simultaneously?"

Question: Regarding the teaching of the Dharma, it is answered that by means of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable transformations, inconceivable power of samādhi, and so forth, hundreds of thousands [of beings] simultaneously engage in speech and silence. Because the śrāvakas are transformed yet do not act as transformations, no transformative activities remain after his parinirvāṇa.
Since the Tathāgata can leave behind transformative activities after his parinirvāṇa that are no different from the Buddha himself, it is therefore called "transformation. Furthermore—
[The Buddha] manifested the form of a hungry ghost. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 16, states:
"Among the hungry ghosts, because of hunger and thirst, both eyes are sunken, their hair and body hair grow long, and they run hither and thither."
When they run toward the water, the deity who guards the water strikes them back with an iron staff; even if there were no guardian deity, the water would naturally dry up.

At times, when it rains from heaven, the rain turns into charcoal. There are also hungry ghosts who are constantly scorched by fire, like during the time of the kalpa-ending conflagration when fires erupt from all the mountains.
Furthermore, there are hungry ghosts who are emaciated and run about frantically, their hair disheveled and matted.
Some cover their bodies with filth; some constantly consume excrement, urine, mucus, saliva, and vomit; some go to the side of latrines to seek out impurities;
some have bodies like scorched trees and throats like the eye of a needle; some split open their own heads to lick the brains;
and some have forms like black mountains with iron chains shackling their heads—all because they were fond of harsh speech in previous lives.
When one utters coarse words and treats others with contempt, everyone loathes them and those who see them regard them as enemies.
Due to this transgression, they fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*); that passage further describes the conditions of the hells in succession. I entreat you to examine and read it:
first, so that you may be cautious and reverent; second, so that you may give rise to a mind of compassion.

Regarding the three grades of precepts, the *Vibhaṣā-śāstra* states: "If one resolves, 'I now seek the Way and shall save all sentient beings,' yet [thinks] that sentient beings merely borrow their life spans and accepts this matter [with such a view], this is the lower grade of a weak mind;
although one has obtained the Buddha-precepts, they are nonetheless not [the true precepts]."
Regarding "superior-excellent," what is the middle grade? It is to say: "I now, with a right mind, turn toward the Way; I resolve the doubts of sentient beings and act as a bridge for all;
I am able to benefit myself and also benefit others, upholding the correct precepts. What is the superior grade? It is to say:
"I now resolve to take up the precepts in order to fulfill the three clusters [of pure conduct] and proceed toward the three gates of liberation."

Those who seek the fruit of Nirvana through the gates, and who likewise use this Dharma to guide and benefit sentient beings so that they may reach Nirvana and cause the Dharma to abide for a long time—
each is categorized as superior, middling, or inferior according to their respective capacity.
Third, regarding the observance of the ritual precepts (*śīla*), there are three grades: the superior grade results in rebirth as a deva; the middling grade results in rebirth as a human;
and the inferior grade results in rebirth as an asura. Furthermore, within the middling grade, there are superior, middling, and inferior levels, which correspond to humans of the four continents.

Moreover, the superior grade has three further divisions, referring to the various ranks among the devas. Regarding the observance of the principle precepts (*śīla*), each of the three—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle (*madhyama*)—also has three grades.

Regarding the three types of emptiness: the lower pertains to the śrāvakas, the middle to the pratyekabuddhas, and the upper to the bodhisattvas. Regarding the three types of provisional [expedient means]:

the lower pertains to the bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka, the middle to the bodhisattvas who have emerged from the provisional, and the upper to the distinct (vaipulya) bodhisattvas. Regarding the three types of purity:
the lower pertains to the distinct bodhisattvas, the middle to the round (perfect) bodhisattvas, and the upper is possessed only by the Buddha. Thus they are endowed with pure precepts.
It should be stated that from the highest-of-the-high grade down to the lowest-of-the-low grade, there are four grades:
the Perfect (yuan) highest-of-the-high, the Distinct (bie) highest, the Common (tong) lower, and the Storehouse (zang) lowest-of-the-low. These four grades correspond to the two vehicles as follows:

the common [storehouse] highest-of-the-high corresponds to the Pratyekabuddha; the common highest corresponds to the Śrāvaka; the storehouse lower corresponds to the Pratyekabuddha; and the storehouse lowest-of-the-low corresponds to the Śrāvaka.
There is no such thing as an isolated occurrence;
within the two verses of the *Saṃghāta-gāthā*, it is not entirely without subject matter. Now, let us specifically identify that which is not explicitly versified within those two verses.
For example, the fourth meaning of the *Gāthā* refers to the analytical discernment of phenomena according to their specific instances.
*Kuai* (pronounced *xi* with the *yang* tone).
This explains the meaning of the following verse.
The character "Śākya" (釋) is used redundantly.

[Xuanzang’s Commentary] When all Buddhas return to their native lands, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (大論), fascicle 33, states that King Śuddhodana caused five hundred Śākyas to renounce the household life. *Muktaka* (目多伽) means "pure" (*viśuddha*). King Śuddhodana commanded five hundred Śākyas to leave the home life.
When he was about to arrive at the city of Śrāvastī, he ordered Śāriputra to deliver [the relics] and subsequently return them to his own country;
the two characters "zhū fó" (諸佛, *zhūfó*) here are likely erroneous. [Note: *yuǎn*] 爰 (yuan).
Lun-yin (the *Śabdavarga*) says that "gǔ" (古) is pronounced like "mài" (麥); it means to take meat while protecting it with one's claws.
"Mǎo" (卯) is pronounced like "mòu" (候); it means to exchange goods.
[Xuanzang’s Translation: "Regarding the gift of the red-eyed fish to those suffering from various ailments, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
'In a past age, when the people were frequently afflicted by diseases such as jaundice and yellowish-white atrophy, the Bodhisattva at that time took birth as a red-eyed fish.
He offered his own flesh to various sick people in order to save them from their illnesses.'"
Regarding "rescuing those drowning in the whirlpool," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the past, the Bodhisattva was born as a bird dwelling in a forest.
He saw a man who had entered deep water and was seized by a water spirit. According to the method of the water spirit’s seizure, it was impossible to untie him. The bird knew how to release him."
When the Dharma arrived at Mount Gandhamādana, he took a medicinal herb and placed it upon his *huàn* (a binding cord); the cord immediately rotted away, allowing him to escape.
Now, Xuánwén writes this as "huàn," which is pronounced like "húquǎn" (the sound of a wild dog).

In the *Lùn* (Treatise), it is written as "huàn," and the phonetic gloss states that it should be written as "guàn" (pronounced like "gǔquǎn"), meaning a rope used for catching beasts. The *Lùn* says: "It rotted away; one knows it was a rope."
The *Benqi yinyuan deng lun* (Treatise on the Origins and Conditions, etc.
states that the *Benqi yinyuan jing*, the *Yun jing*, the *Fayun jing*, and the *Dayun jing* each consist of one hundred thousand verses;
this is also distinguished within the "Resolving Doubts" section.
He says: "If one gradually opens [the fist], four emerge—just as opening a fist produces fingers; there are only fingers and no fist.
If one closes the four together, they become gradual—as closing the fingers forms a fist; there is only the fist and no fingers remain. If the gradual is maintained, the teaching has only four;
if the gradual is eliminated, the teaching has only seven. If both are maintained, one side must lack substance. To establish eight, the substance would be narrow while the name would be broad."
Regarding the number of verses and chapters:
the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-śāstra* (Huayan lun xu) states that the Sūtra consists of three sections.
The first section contains as many verses as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, and as many chapters as there are atoms in a world-system of four continents. The middle section... [text continues]
There were originally four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses in one thousand two hundred chapters;
however, one section consisting of one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters was not transmitted to the world.

The Venerable Nāgārjuna, while traveling through the ocean treasury, observed that the first two sections were not what had been passed down, and thus he recited the latter section and returned to the Five Indies.
If one were to first expound the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there is a fear that it might increase false inversions;
for if one initially speaks of the nature of phenomena as being spontaneously so, it would increase the conceptualization of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
In both cases, the Bodhisattvas...

This is a passage that harmonizes two textual sections. The first states: "It directly explicates the conventional reality of conceptual thought (*cintya-saṃvṛti*)," referring to this conventional reality in conjunction with that of the Two Vehicles.
The second states: "If it is for the sake of the *piṭaka*-based bodhisattvas, it is the conventional reality of conceptual thought," which distinguishes it from the former.
Although these two passages differ slightly, both treat the conventional as primary and the ultimate as secondary; therefore, they are specifically mentioned.
Other examples may be understood by reflecting upon the first phrase.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra* commentary explains: "The Tripiṭaka clarifies the coarse and subtle five aggregates as having the meaning of 'this is suffering' and 'this is not suffering.

In the Mahāyāna gate, one realizes that fundamentally there is no suffering of coarse or subtle nature; it exists only because of deluded vision. When one perceives the essence, it is immediately empty, and thus it is not seen."

The characteristic of suffering is called "non-arising," which is the very meaning of suffering. In the Tripiṭaka, the two kinds of emptiness—the emptiness of dharmas and the emptiness of persons—are clarified;

this is merely the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), not the meaning of ultimate emptiness. In the Mahāyāna gate, one realizes that the essence is *tathatā* (suchness) and the true mark; there is no need for further refutation or analysis, as this is the meaning of true emptiness.
In the Tripiṭaka, the clarification of "no-self" refers to a selflessness that is not [absolute] non-self; this is the meaning in the Mahāyāna gate.
In the true mark of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there has from the beginning been neither self nor non-self; these two have never been dual.
This non-duality is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature is precisely the meaning of true non-self.

What is elucidated in the Tripiṭaka—that returning from existence to non-existence is called *nirvāṇa* as quiescent extinction—is the meaning of "extinction" rather than the meaning of "non-extinction. The Mahāyāna school elucidates all... [text truncated]
That all phenomena have from the very beginning been characterized by constant quiescence is the meaning of Great Nirvana, which is the principle of true quiescence.
That from the beginning there has been neither birth-and-death nor Nirvana, and that the principle of non-duality between arising-extinction and true emptiness is the meaning of true quiescence.
"Why do the concluding phrases all revert to the four 'withered' states, stating that these are impermanent and so forth?

This is the meaning of the text within the commentary (*śāstra*). His response says: "If one breaks through the True [Nature] to enter the Middle, then the conclusion regarding the True establishes it as withered;
within the Middle, it naturally becomes flourishing. As the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies, two birds fly together: permanence and impermanence are both the True and the impermanent."
The meaning cannot be separated from the "gradual.
It is called "gradual" because, for example, Vimalakīrti used the five meanings of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) to reprimand Candra-kumārabhūta. Thus, it is termed "gradual."

Sudden [Awakening] is as stated in the *Śūnyatā-saṃbhava Sūtra*: "If Subhūti does not sever ignorance and craving, yet does not dwell together with them; if he does not destroy the body, yet conforms to the single mark;
if he does not extinguish ignorance and craving, yet gives rise to clarity and liberation—then by means of the marks of the five heinous crimes, one attains liberation."
Only then may one partake of this food; for this reason, it is called "sudden" (dùn), as it is a complete negation (yúánhē).
The two birds flying together is as cited in the commentary on the tenth fascicle of the *Zhujing yixiang*.

First, the conventional follows the three truths by revolving through the illusory existence as the conventional and the illusory existence as emptiness as the truth; this is the conventional revolving through the general truth.

Furthermore, illusory existence as the conventional and illusory existence as both emptiness and non-emptiness together as the truth; this is the conventional revolving through the specific truth. Furthermore, the illusory...
Conditioned phenomena are conventionally illusory existence, which is both empty and not empty; that all dharmas tend toward emptiness and non-emptiness is the ultimate truth.
This conventional truth shifts according to the perfection of the ultimate truth.
Of this ultimate truth, there are only two [aspects].
The emptiness of the ultimate truth and the middle truth.
Regarding the twelve divisions of the sutras on contemplating the mind:
there are those who have heard of them but not yet seen them; I shall now briefly summarize them here. They state that contemplating the mind is itself emptiness.
The provisional, the middle, and the true are the direct explanation of names; this is *sūtra*. Repeatedly contemplating the mind as empty, provisional, and middle is *geya*.

Contemplating the mind as empty and giving rise to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñā*) is the provisional; giving rise to the knowledge of the paths and their varieties (*mārgajñatā*) is the middle;

giving rise to the single mind and the three knowledges is the *vaipulya*. Receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) while contemplating the mind as empty, provisional, and middle is likewise [the *avadāna*].

The contemplation of the mind as emptiness is itself provisional; within emptiness, it is also provisional. The contemplation of the mind as provisionality is itself empty; within provisionality, it is also empty. Emptiness and provisionality are themselves the middle. This is called the verse on the non-dual naming:

"The contemplation of the mind as emptiness, provisionality, and the middle is without distinction. It is not that there is prior thought followed by subsequent awakening; this is called the unasked spontaneous teaching.

One should contemplate that every single moment of mind necessarily arises in dependence upon conditions; this very arising through causes and conditions is itself emptiness, provisionality, and the middle. This is called "arising from causes and conditions."
The three characteristics of abiding, ceasing, and arising existing within a single moment of mind—namely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—are likewise so.

This is called the Contemplation of the Mind as Analogy; that the nature and virtues of the mind are empty, provisional, and middle is also the principle of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

That the beginning and end of cultivated virtue are also empty, provisional, and middle is called the Contemplation of the Mind as the Fundamental Reality. From the realms above hell upward, [they are likewise so].
Reaching the Buddhas, that which is emptiness, the provisional, and the middle is called the Contemplation of the Original Birth of the Mind as Emptiness, Provisionality, and Middle;

it extends horizontally throughout the Dharma-realm and penetrates vertically to Bodhi, and is thus called the Contemplation of the Mind as Emptiness, Provisionality, and Middle in the Vaipulya (Extensive) sense. Furthermore, this contemplation of the mind as emptiness, provisionality, and middle is also the Contemplation of the Unprecedented.
Because the mind is empty and arises from conditions, and because all conditions are non-arising, it is therefore empty. Why is it empty?
That which is provisionally designated as "emptiness of emptiness" consists merely of words; since these words are provisional constructs, emptiness itself is provisional.

Provisionality and emptiness do not transcend the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Since the nature of phenomena is itself the Middle Way and is identical to emptiness, it should not be grasped as being merely provisional.
Thus, the non-interruption [of this realization] is the Middle Way. To investigate and examine in this manner is called "discursive analysis" (*viniścaya*).
"Capable" refers to the retinue;
"should act" means one should mount the horse. I pray that you may do so.
In a past kalpa, when the Buddha was a prince practicing the Way in the mountains as a king’s son, Śakra Devendra transformed himself into a monkey and said to the prince:
"Excellent! When you attain Buddhahood, I beg to become a horse to carry you."
It is also like the case of Prince Mahānāma, who, having delighted in giving during his time as Prince Mahānāma under a former Buddha, was banished by his father the King and placed in Mount Tāṇḍaka.
There dwelt a practitioner named Acchuta, five hundred years of age; the Prince paid him homage. Acchuta—
He then asked, "What do you seek? The Prince replied, "I seek the Mahāyāna.
Cunda said, "When the Prince attains the Unsurpassed Way, may I become his foremost disciple in supernatural powers;
I am the one known as Maudgalyāyana."
[Xuanzang’s Translation: Devadatta is [the one whose name] appears as Piṅgala in the Mahāyāna treatises;
Ajātaśatru is [the one whose name is] Acala.
The *Pǔchāojīng* (Sūtra on Universal Transcendence) states that King Ajātaśatru, having repented before Mañjuśrī, attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
At the end of his life, he entered the Piṇḍala hell; yet upon entering, he was immediately reborn in the upper realms, where he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When Maitreya appears in the world, he will return to this realm under the name of Bodhisattva Acala.
The *Satyaka-nirgrantha-mahopāya-satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra* states:
"In my Buddha-land, there are various non-Buddhist followers of the Nirgranthas;
all of them exist by the power of the Tathāgata, for the purpose of manifesting the inconceivable realm of skillful means. All [of these]...
All non-Buddhists abide in the gate of inconceivable liberation;
Pāpīyān,
on the contrary, is an evil one.
[Xuanzang]: Pronounced "cu" (six tones).
[Xuanzang]: Puxian Bodhisattva.

In the sūtra, the Bodhisattva Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana states that the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) differ according to their respective categories, each opening up the three gates of liberation and the practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā;
thus, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment lead to the city of the untainted (anāsrava), which has three gates and contains three gates.
The "Suffering" section below [the first] is the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); the four lines below "Cessation" (*nirodha*) are the gate of signlessness (*animitta*);

the eight lines below "Origination" (*samudaya*) and "Path" (*mārga*), along with the two lines below "Suffering," are the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Regarding that which penetrates these three gates: suffering and origination are like illusions and transformations—this is the gate of emptiness;
knowing emptiness and yet having no perception of emptiness—this is the gate of signlessness; although the perception of emptiness is absent, one still calculates...

Since the wisdom of contemplation is devoid of subject and object, who could perform the contemplation of emptiness? This is called the Gate of Non-Action (*anabhisamskāra*). To distinguish these three gates:

entering from the conventional into emptiness is called the Samādhi of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*); knowing that emptiness is not [ultimately] empty and emerging into the conventional to transform sentient beings without any further marks of emptiness is called the Gate of Signlessness (*animitta-mukha*);
progressing in the cultivation of the Middle Way without seeking either the middle or the extremes is called the Gate of Non-Action. These are the three gates of the Perfect [Teaching].

This is the single emptiness wherein all things are empty; one does not perceive the characteristics of the distinctions between the four gates. It is neither true nor conditioned, and there is no agent who creates it.
This is also as recorded in the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation), which further cites the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

Regarding the statement that the five heinous acts (*pañcānantarya*) are explained in terms of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*): because these five dharmas oppose the world, they are called the "five heinous acts.

As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "If one kills the father of ignorance, harms the mother of craving, cuts off the enemy of sleep, destroys the harmony of the aggregates (*skandha*), and severs the body of the seven consciousnesses—if there is such a doer, they will realize and manifest the true Dharma."
Regarding the three types of contemplation—karma, vow, and supernatural power—their arising is all without exception the contemplation of mental karma.
The contemplation of karma arises when the three contemplations serve as the resources that manifest the Dharma-body.

The contemplation of vows arises when the mental factors are themselves empty, provisional, and middle, thereby uniting with the Middle Way. The contemplation of supernatural powers arises through the inconceivable application of the three secrets. The contemplation of response arises accordingly.
The characteristics of the wisdom of the truths are darkly interfused; each is identical with emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
This is the contemplation of phenomena based on objective events (*karmādhiṣṭhāna-vastu-pratītya-dhyāna*).

While the path of contemplation establishes designations in relation to phenomena, it does not exclusively concern the contemplation of the mind through doctrinal categories (*dharma-mukha*). The "Father of Expedient Means" and the "Mother of Prajñāpāramitā" are precisely examples of this, as they refer solely to the mind. However—
Since the objects of inquiry—such as parents, wives, children, and even carriages—are manifold, one's contemplation cannot be focused on a single point;
yet, if it were to be focused, one would focus exclusively on emptiness, the provisional, and the middle within a single object.
Neither horizontally nor vertically can they reach it;
Kāśyapa’s understanding was limited only to the Two Vehicles, let alone the fact that all ten dharma-realms equally attain the Buddha-way.

As for the remaining eight dharma-realms, they do not enter the scope of his words—this is what is meant by "not reached horizontally. Furthermore, the seven stages of expedient means proceed from shallow to deep, all...
Entering into true wisdom, the remaining five skillful means are entirely beyond verbal expression; this is what is meant by being "vertically unattainable. Regarding the term *ānantarya*:

some say it is the nose (*nāsikā*), while others say it is the root (*mūla*); these are merely differences in the *Chūxià* (northern) and *Fàn* (Sanskrit) pronunciations, like the difference between the *Huá* (Chinese) and foreign sounds. In the Chinese language, it means "uninterrupted" (*wújiàn*), "without obstruction" (*wúzhé*), and "without... [repetition of the last character].

In the Black Rope Hell, they first measure the limbs and bodies with black ropes, and only afterwards are they cut and sawed; furthermore, it is said that these sentient beings are moved by their own karma."
Iron chains, shaped like black cords, saw them apart; furthermore, the sinews and veins of those sentient beings were all transformed into black cords that sawed them asunder.
[In the] Saṃghāta [hell], they are crushed together.

When those sentient beings are surrounded by many instruments of suffering that come together to oppress their bodies, and when they are about to undergo such suffering, mountains close in from all sides at once; it is for this reason that it is so named.
The eight *utsada* (supplementary hells) are all sixteen;
outside each of the four gates of the eight *naraka*s, there are four, namely the four such as the Pit of Hot Ashes (*kukūla*).
The first is the Pit of Hot Ashes.

This refers to the "Hot Ashes" (Kukūla) hell. The hot ashes reach up to the knees; when sentient beings enter it, as soon as they set foot down, their skin, flesh, and blood are all scorched and rotted away.
When they lift their feet, they are restored to their former state once again.
Second, the Hell of Excrement:
this hell is filled with excrement and filth, within which there are worms with beaks as sharp as needles that pierce the bones and eat the marrow.
Third, the Hell of Razor Blades.
In this hell, knives and swords are spread out overhead to form a great path; when sentient beings set foot upon it, their skin and flesh are shattered and severed.
Furthermore, there is a forest of sword-leaves where the wind blows the sword-leaves against their bodies, causing their bones and flesh to fall away.

There is also a forest of sword-thorns with iron spikes; when those sentient beings are forced to climb the trees, the thorns point downward, and when they are forced to descend, the thorns point upward.

When they climb the trees, the thorns point upward; these thorns are sharp and piercing, so that as soon as they prick their limbs, their hearts and livers are torn apart, and various iron-beaked insects swarm and scramble to devour them.
[Next is] the River of Fourfold Heat.
This hell is filled with hot, brackish water; when sentient beings enter it, they float and sink, their bones and flesh steamed and boiled until they fall apart,
like beans or rice being cooked in a large cauldron filled with lye while a fierce fire burns beneath it,
causing the beans and rice to swirl incessantly within the vessel.

The "Supplementary Explanations" (*Upapadaka*) refer to the supplementary hells (*utsada-naraka*). They are called "supplementary" because they are filled with [the following]: the *Kukūla* (Embers) hell, which is filled with embers reaching up to the knees;
the *Kuṇapa* (Feces) hell, which is filled with a mire of excrement and filth; and the *Asipatravana* (Sword-Leaf Forest) hell, which consists of blades.
This is because the Forest of Swords, the Forest of Iron Thorns, and the Forest of Sword-leaves increase [in severity].
*Zhāzhà*:
the sound of *zhā* is *zhé*, and *zhà* is pronounced *zhéjiā* (or *zhèjià*). Because the cold is so extreme that one cannot open one's mouth, one can only...

If [the karma] were to arise only when one has already attained rebirth in hell— as if there were a specific organ within hell— then even a noble being (ārya) would cause others to slander the Dharma and fall into hell,
as was the case with the conditions involving Jayamati.

Furthermore, it is only when one destroys the outflows (*āsrava*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of the cultivation of the king of untainted (*anāsrava*) samādhis that it is finally destroyed.
The preceding three [realms] are fully described as in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*.
By observing the precept against killing, one is reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; by observing the precepts against killing and stealing, one is reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
and by adding the precept against sexual misconduct, one is reborn in the Yāma Heaven.

According to the Sarvāstivādins, it is established that acquisitions (prāpti) are acquired by subsequent acquisitions;
because the subsequent acquisition acquires the prior acquisition, it enables past karma to reach the future body. When the acquisition of death has ceased, the future retribution arises.
Just as a single karma is established through one great acquisition, and because the dharma-characteristics of the karma continue in succession without interruption, it is called a "rope" (rajjū).
[Xuanzang]: *Tāotùe* (饕餮):

The sixteen types of evil disciplines (*akuśala-saṃvara*) are:

"This means that if one entrusts these precious objects to you, and when I return on another day, all the items entrusted by this old man have been entirely lost... (and so forth)... even to the point of saying:

Because all things are impermanent, just like that old man, the Buddha-dharma should be entrusted to the bodhisattvas so that it may endure for a long time,
just like that strong man who received another’s deposit of one hundred pieces of gold. Zhan’an says this is a metaphor for the hundred phrases of liberation.
To explain extensively how they protect the Dharma:
those who claim to uphold the True Dharma yet do not receive the five precepts or various disciplinary codes, and instead carry swords, blades,

Among the Ten Subtleties, since these [examples] are coarse, they use this coarseness to refute the ten types of coarseness—such as the objects, wisdom, and practice—of the Three Teachings.

It is also "this dharma";

Initially, the opening based on the object is according to principle;
as it says in the section on the object of the twelve links of dependent origination: "How could there be a coarse difference between the conceivable and the inconceivable?"

the "body" refers to what is said as either one's own body or another's body;
the opening up of the "matter" refers to what is shown as either one's own matter or another's matter.

as for others who have not yet destroyed ignorance, [the same principle applies].

The twenty-two [verses] state that the three seals are explained extensively as four and briefly as one: first, all conditioned phenomena arise and perish moment by moment and are thus impermanent;

All elements (dhātus) are conditioned phenomena characterized by arising and ceasing; they existed previously but do not exist now, and exist now but will not exist later.

All phenomena are without self (*anātman*); within all phenomena there is no master, no agent, no knower, no seer, no one who is born, and no doer.
All phenomena belong to causes and conditions; because they belong to causes and conditions, they lack independence; because they lack independence, they are non-existent.

For what reason do you speak only of impermanence and the non-self of all phenomena? Answer: Because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) have no cause and no condition, they are neither born nor extinguished.

For this reason, it is not said that these are impermanent; rather, it can be said that there is no self (*anātman*). Some people claim that the *puruṣa* (self) is eternal and possesses the characteristic of universal knowledge.
For this reason, it is taught that among all phenomena there is no self, and that which is quiescent is *nirvāṇa*.
Because the fires of the three poisons have been extinguished, it is called the Seal of Quiescence (*śānti-mudrā*). Question: Within the Seal of Quiescence, why is there only a single dharma?

It is not said that there are many answers; rather, in the first seal it is taught that there are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); in the second seal it is taught that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*);

If one says that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are impermanent, then the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*) and external things such as the five desires are destroyed. If one speaks of non-self, then the internal self and the dharma-self (*dharmanairātmya*) are destroyed.

Because it is that which is to be destroyed, it is called "quiescent nirvāṇa. When a practitioner contemplates conditioned phenomena as impermanent, they give rise to world-weariness regarding suffering.

The single characteristic is what is called "characteristiclessness. How is it that herein all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are said to be impermanent, and this is termed the "Seal of the Dharma" (*dharma-mudrā*)?
Why do these two dharmas not contradict one another? Answer: Contemplating impermanence is the causal condition for contemplating emptiness.
For example, when one contemplates that form (*rūpa*) is impermanent from moment to moment, one thereby knows it to be empty; because past form has ceased and perished, it cannot [be apprehended].
Because it is seen, there is no characteristic of form; because future form does not arise, is unconditioned, useless, and invisible, there is no characteristic of form.
Because present form also does not abide, is invisible, and cannot be known through discrimination, there is no characteristic of form.
This absence of the characteristic of form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself non-arising and non-ceasing. That which is non-arising and non-ceasing is, in its reality, suchness.

Regarding the otter’s ritual in the second month, the *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) of the *Record of Rites* (*Liji*) states: "The otter catches fish to sacrifice to Heaven; therefore, in the second month, during the 'Vital Energy' (*zhongqi*) period, the otter sacrifices to Heaven with fish."

Both the *chai* and the otter are used as sacrificial offerings so that the Son of Heaven may maintain reverence for the ancestral temple.

Regarding the "nets on three sides," the *Shiji* records that when Tang went out and saw nets spread across the wilds with openings on four sides, he offered a prayer, saying: "From the heavens above and from the four directions..."

In the final years of the Jiaping era, [Zhang Daoling] was swallowed by a python. His son, Zhang Heng, rushed out but could find no trace of him;

It is said that one may clarify the three truths by way of the gate of existence (*astitva-mukha*), like a blind person hearing a conch shell; or one may clarify the three [truths] by way of the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*).

The Three Truths are elucidated through the gate of existence (you-men) like a blind person hearing the sound of rice flour; they are elucidated through the gate of emptiness (kong-men) like a blind person hearing snow;

and they are elucidated through the gate of the double negation (shuang-fei) like a blind person hearing a crane. The *Fuxing* commentary explains: "Although the sound of the conch is empty, the substance of the conch is real"—this serves as a metaphor for the gate of existence.

In the "Tathāgatagarbha" chapter of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, it is asked: "Why is the Buddha-nature difficult to see and difficult to enter? The Buddha replied:

He pointed with one finger and asked, "Do you see? He replied, "I do not see. He then pointed with two fingers and three fingers and asked, "Do you see?
He replied, "I see a little. Zhan’an’s commentary explains: he used the Three Truths as the three fingers.

Pointing with the first finger symbolizes the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha-satya*); [the disciple] does not see the middle nature. Pointing with two fingers symbolizes the two truths of Ultimate Reality and the Conventional (*saṃvṛti-satya*); likewise, [he does not see].

The metaphor of the three fingers for seeing the nature illustrates that one truth is itself the three truths; thus it is said that "seeing even a little" refers to the stage of the Ten Abidings (*daśabhūmi*).

Visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility constitute the true nature [of things], while "hair-fraction" (*vālāgra*) is a conventional designation. A "hair-fraction" refers to a minute portion within a hair;
therefore, even atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth are called hair-fractions because they are aggregations of hairs. Thus, they are termed "wool" (*ūrṇā*).

(And so forth. Once this milk has ceased, through what causes and conditions does it become curd? Whether it be acidity or warmth—these are the causes and conditions.

[Xuanzang’s Commentary]: Regarding the realization of the distinct wisdoms of the Perfect Gate (*pariccheda-mukha*), there are two possibilities:

either the Perfect Wisdom (*pariccheda-jñāna*) is explained first, in which case this refers to the stage after the stage of faith (*śraddhā*); or the Sequential Wisdom (*anupūrva-jñāna*) is explained first, in which case this refers to the stage prior to the stages of abiding (*vihāra*).

Alternatively, the Sequential Wisdom is explained first, referring to the stage prior to the stages of abiding, and the Perfect Wisdom is explained later, referring to the stage after the stages of abiding. Thus, the Perfect and Sequential [wisdoms] follow one another.
Furthermore, because the meanings of "knowledge" (*jñāna*) differ, they are distinguished by separate gates. In some cases, the fruits are explained as not being sequential;

in others, the fruits are first clarified as being sequential. In this [present] explanation, the fruits of the stages (*bhūmi*) are clarified as being non-sequential, while the fruits of the paths of application (*prayoga*) are explained as being sequential.
First, it clarifies that the fruit is not sequential; this teaching refers to the subsequent stages. Alternatively, it clarifies that the fruit is sequential;
this teaching refers to the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*).

The preceding clarification of the fruit being "transverse" (縱) refers to the dwelling [of the fruit] before and after; this does not clarify the fruit being "longitudinal" (縱). However, the subsequent clarification of faith does not refer to the fruit being "longitudinal.

In truth, both cause and effect of the perfect virtues arise from the nature (性), and neither are transverse nor longitudinal. It is only for the sake of distinguishing their respective categories that we speak of transverse and longitudinal here.

This reveals that the four "withered" aspects are fundamentally the four "flourishing" aspects. To speak of the four "withered" aspects refers to the fact that the very substance of birth-and-death is entirely nirvana; thus it is called "withered.

Each contains the text of nine sections concerning the characteristics of the middle gate from the introductory preface;

The *Commentary on Stopping and Contemplation* (*Zhiguan ji*) contains a detailed sub-commentary;
I shall now cite that text to annotate this work, so that those who study and practice may avoid the trouble of cross-referencing.

It is like a wealthy elder (the Buddha), who possesses many oxen (the teachings); though their colors are various (according to individual capacities), they all belong to a single herd (the unity of principle).

He entrusted the cowherd (the propagator of the teaching) with the task of following the water and grass (to suit the capacities of beings), seeking only the finest cream (the eternal *dharmakāya*), and not the milk or curd (the realms of humans, devas, and the two vehicles).
At that time, the cowherd, having milked the cows, ate it himself (the propagator of the teaching benefits himself).

When the elder passed away (the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa*), all the cows were plundered by a band of thieves (those who steal the Buddha’s Dharma). Having obtained the cows, the thieves had no women among them (they lacked compassion).

[The ox] having already consumed [the offerings] for himself, the bandits said to one another: "This elder keeps this ox solely for the sake of the clarified butter (sarpis), not seeking milk or curd.
By what means can we obtain it? [They were filled with] longing. "We have no vessels (anindriya); even if we were to obtain the milk, we would have no place to store it.
[Even if they maintained the precepts, they would not abide permanently in their original state. Again, they said to one another: "Only a leather bag can contain it. [Humans and devas...]

Although the vessel containing the curdled milk (*āmiṣa-phala*) is present, if one does not know how to churn it, the whey will still be difficult to obtain; how much more so for the cream and butter? (Lacking concentration, wisdom, and skillful means is called "not knowing how to churn";

if even the semblance of the Way is absent, how much less the true and eternal? At that time, the bandits, for the sake of the clarified butter (*sarpis*), added water to it (giving rise to false views).
Because of the excess of water, everything was lost (giving rise to views and falling into evil states, thereby losing the fruits of human and celestial realms).
The above are all notes from the *Fuxing-zhu* (Commentary on the *Sifenlü Xingshichao*). Master Nanshan said:
"In ancient times, when the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was lectured upon, there was only a single fascicle of commentary; later, the Dharma Master [Zhiyan] composed a three-fascicle commentary.

In the present day, those who lecture on it produce ten fascicles of commentary for even a single chapter such as the 'Ten Stages' (*Daśabhūmi*), each vying to display their own capabilities and competing to manifest flowery rhetoric; the words and characters are so vast and extensive that they serve merely as a vessel for the mind."
At this time, fools compete to seek out names rather than the Dharma; since one should not even cling to the Dharma, how much less should one cling to its words?
Thus, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "The scriptural text is one, yet the lecturers provide divergent explanations.

Each relying on their own views, they corrupt and disrupt the True Dharma. Because the celestial deities become incensed, the three calamities arise together. For these reasons, [the teaching has declined].
The Buddha-dharma is as insipid as a peck of water mixed with a pint of curd; it may appear to have the color of curd, yet when eaten, it has no flavor.
Reflecting deeply upon these expositions and human sentiments, one realizes that the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom is something no human can fathom.
The above are the instructions bestowed by Master Nanshan. Furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* warns people against excessive and forced interpretation.

You must first clarify the horizontal and vertical dimensions, and subsequently clarify non-duality.

As it says in the section on the "Object of Cultivated Virtue": "When the mind arises, it must necessarily rely upon conditions; is it the mind that possesses [the conditions], or are the conditions possessed by the mind, or are they both?"
One should know that when seeking the mind through the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) of "possessing" and "being devoid of," it cannot be found;

likewise, the three thousand [realms] (*trisāhasra*) also cannot be found—these are the four horizontal permutations. Furthermore, it is said: since they are obtained horizontally, should the three thousand arise and perish in a single thought-moment?
Whether arising and perishing, or neither perishing nor not perishing—the arising of the three thousand is in all cases unobtainable; this is the vertical [permutation].
Neither vertical nor horizontal, it is likewise unattainable—this is non-duality. Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states:

"The inconceivable realm that reaches the bottom of the true reality is called 'vertical'; that which encompasses the ten dharma realms is called 'horizontal. To aspire upward from the mind is called 'vertical,' and to transform downward is called 'horizontal.
Moreover, aspiring upward and transforming downward is called 'vertical,' while relying on the realm to arouse vows is called 'horizontal. This refers to the "settling of the mind" (*anxin*).

The ultimate principle is called "vertical" (*ūrdhva*); the sixty-four stages are called "horizontal" (*tiryak*). Even the entry into the stage of non-attachment is called "vertical," while being free from the three semblances of phenomena is called "horizontal.
Furthermore, when discussing each of the ten [stages] in relation to one another, it is called "horizontal," and reaching the ultimate limit of each is called "vertical.
The true reality (*dharmatā*) of each is neither horizontal nor vertical; when both horizontal and vertical are simultaneously negated, that is [the state of] non-duality.
Secondly, it is only upon reaching the final two chapters that one can enter into the principle;
these two chapters are as previously noted: the Chapter on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination and the Chapter on Refuting Erroneous Views.

First, regarding the introductory sections of the three cycles and seven parables, all begin by recounting the past. For example, in the "Parable" chapter (*Upamā-parivarta*), the past is recounted through the three vehicles;

regarding the three types of cultivation— namely, the inferior, the superior, and the excellent— the inferior refers to the continuity of mundane inverted views, which perceive [the impermanent] as permanent.

That which is agreeable and pleasing is called "pleasure" (*sukha*); that which moves, shifts, and functions is called "self" (*ātman*). Being shrouded by ignorance (*moha*), one reaps no benefit whatsoever.
Inferior persons rely on the teachings of the "half-syllables" (*ardhakṣara*) to destroy false attachments: they destroy permanence with impermanence, pleasure with suffering, and self with non-self;
[they hold that] the three realms are all impermanent, all states of existence are entirely without pleasure, and everything is empty and without self.
The Victorious Ones, relying on the supreme teaching of the Buddha, refute inferior practices—namely, those that conceive of the *dharmakāya* as being permanent, blissful, and possessing a self.

Instead, they teach that it is eternally constant and without change, dwelling within the treasury of awakening (*bodhigarbha*), experiencing joy and delight, endowed with the eight masteries (*aṣṭavaśitā*), and incapable of being obstructed.
Those who practice in this manner enter the secret treasury; this is called the supreme third practice.

The texts of the Four Teachings are fundamentally divided into four propositions;
although each of the Four Teachings possesses its own fourfold analysis, their essential names and definitive realities are merely these four.
I shall now further cite those texts to demonstrate them, so that this passage may be easily understood. It says: "The Tripitaka is the teaching that expounds impermanence."

These three vehicles equally receive the teaching for entering the Way, which constitutes both the general and the specific; that which is taught for Bodhisattvas—the great vows and the six perfections—constitutes the specific teaching.
That which leads one into the fruit of Buddhahood through the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) constitutes the perfect and comprehensive teaching.

When the teacher speaks of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, is this not the Path-knowledge (*mārgajñatā*) of the Tripiṭaka teaching? Is it not the specific teaching that speaks of the knowledge of all modes?
Is it not the case that both the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) and the Separate Teaching (Biejiao) speak of precepts, concentration, and wisdom; speak of the principle of the non-arising of phenomena;
and speak of the Middle Way and the Knowledge of All Modes? The Perfect Teaching also speaks of precepts, concentration, and wisdom;
it possesses the principle of true emptiness, and it likewise possesses distinct, sequential stages and gateways of the Dharma. Thus, although the four teachings have four names...
Furthermore, by cross-referencing and investigating their principles, it is clear that the names established in the teachings must not be confused or conflated.

Regarding the extent of meeting Buddhas, the *Catuḥpratisaraṇa-parivarta* (Chapter on the Four Reliances) states: "If there are sentient beings who, in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River, resolve upon Bodhi..."
Having focused the mind, one will then not slander this sutra amidst the evil world, yet will be unable to analyze and expound it for others (the first *gaṅgā*).
One may possess correct understanding and faith and delight, yet be unable to expound it (the second *gaṅgā*).

One may receive, uphold, copy, and recite it, yet though speaking it for others, fail to understand its profound meaning (the third *gaṅgā*). One may explain it extensively, yet understand only one part out of sixteen (the fourth *gaṅgā*).

As clarified previously, the "essence" (tī) refers to the true nature of the Middle Way among the Ten Profound Subtleties (*daśa-sūkṣmatā*).

The preceding text states that "that which correctly reveals the essence" is precisely the Seal of the Single Real Phase (*eka-bhūta-lakṣaṇa-mudrā*). Within the seventh [category], the Two Truths, the Middle Way is taken as the essence;

subsequently, within the Profundity of Wisdom (*jñāna-sūkṣmatā*), it is distinguished from all else, and so on, until each of the Ten Profound Subtleties individually distinguishes and extracts the correct essence.

rather, the mutual integration within the "abodes" (*vihāra*) represents the perfect [teaching] in its abiding, while the sequential progression after the abodes represents the perfect [teaching] connecting with the distinct [teaching].
The "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings" is a eulogy of the Great Sūtra which says:
"For example, it is like a magician seeing the person he has conjured; a bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings in this same way.
It is like a wise person seeing the moon in water, or the reflection of a face in a mirror, or a mirage in the heat."

The commentary states: "The phrase 'the sound of the call' and so forth, up to 'the Bodhisattva observes sentient beings in this manner,' now explains the meaning of both the Shared (Tong) and Complete (Yuan) Teachings.
The passage praising Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti and others is precisely a commendation of the Complete Teaching."
The Sūtra states: Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "That superior person is difficult to engage in dialogue;

he has profoundly realized the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), skillfully expounds the essential points of the Dharma, possesses unimpeded eloquence, and his wisdom is without obstruction. This is a comprehensive praise of Vimalakīrti.
Upon Mañjuśrī’s entry into the room, Vimalakīrti said, "Welcome, Mañjuśrī; you do not come from the aspect of 'coming'."
He came, yet we did not see his physical form; rather, we saw Mañjuśrī. He said, "O layman, if he has already come, he does not come again;
if he has already gone, he does not go again. Why is this? That which comes comes from nowhere;
that which goes goes nowhere. What can be seen cannot be seen again. This is the perfect praise of Mañjuśrī. [The *Sūtra Commentary* explains: "If..."
If one comes with the characteristic of coming, it is not a "welcome arrival. Now, because Mañjuśrī comes with the characteristic of non-coming, he is praised as having arrived "well.
Why is this? If ordinary beings all possess craving and views, they come by grasping at signs;
if Śrāvakas have shattered the conventional to enter the ultimate, they come by following a devious path to grasp at the partial truth of phenomena. [Mañjuśrī’s coming is different from these.]
The Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka [Vehicle] come having subdued their fetters but have not yet severed the grasping of marks;

the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching come from seeing the true within the provisional by means of its essence, entering the stage of vision and proceeding up to the Bodhisattva stages, coming with these marks of the two truths;
the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching come from the initial mind through the successive traversal of the three truths, entering the first stage—these all rely upon the three truths.

They come with signs; all such cases are not "coming with the sign of non-coming. If one understands the fourfold ineffability according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), one does not perceive signs yet is able to contemplate the Middle Way.
Through unconditioned great compassion (*nirālambana-mahāmaitrī*), one transforms the sentient beings of the *dharmadhātu* so that they all come together to the Land of Tranquil Light.
This is what is meant by "coming with the sign of non-coming. Question: What is the difference between "coming" and "seeing"? Answer: [See response below].

Coming refers to the three wisdoms, and seeing refers to the five eyes; with one mind and three wisdoms, looking back from the fruit toward the cause, the mind-mind is quiescent and naturally flows into the great ocean of wondrous enlightenment. Therefore it is said, "coming in the aspect of not coming.
When the five eyes become increasingly clear until reaching the stage of fruition, one perceives the Dharma-realm in its totality; hence it is said, "seeing in the aspect of not seeing."
Regarding the use of the three teachings, as in the passage where [the Buddha] reproaches Maudgalyāyana, this praises the Mahāyāna;
whereas previously it was said that these three teachings exclude the *Āgamas*, here it is said they praise the Great Sūtra.

The Sūtra says that Maudgalyāyana preached the Dharma to a layperson, but the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra states: "One should not preach the Dharma as you, O worthy one, have done. For one who preaches the Dharma is without preaching and without..."
He shows those who listen to the Dharma that there is neither hearing nor attainment, like a phantom person preaching the Dharma for phantom people;

this is the reprimand using the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sādhāraṇa-yāna*). Furthermore, he says, "One should understand that the faculties of sentient beings have both sharpness and dullness, and one should be skillful in knowledge and vision without any obstruction";
this is the reprimand using the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-bhūmi-yāna*). Furthermore, he says, "With a heart of great compassion, one should offer praise."
To first contemplate repaying the Buddha’s kindness within the Mahāyāna, ensuring that the Three Jewels are never interrupted, and only thereafter expounding the Dharma—
this is the reprimand according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). This is like the reprimand of Śāriputra, which is in fact a praise of the Perfect [Teaching].
The previous passage spoke of disparaging the Tripitaka, while the present one speaks of praising the Perfect [Teaching]; this has already been annotated.

Regarding compassion, vows, and practice, as stated in the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter, Mañjuśrī asked the householder: "What is the cause from which this illness arises? How long has it existed? And how shall it be extinguished?"
Vimalakīrti replied: "My illness arises from ignorance and craving; because all sentient beings are ill, I am ill.
If all sentient beings were free from illness, then my illness would cease. He continued: "One should take one's own illness to have compassion for the illnesses of others;
one should recognize the suffering of countless kalpas in past lives and keep in mind the practice of generosity."
"Benefiting all sentient beings, one should act as a King of Physicians to cure all their ailments," and so forth.
In the "Chapter on the Buddha-way," Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "How does a bodhisattva penetrate the Buddha-way? He replied, "If a bodhisattva..."
He practices the five acts of immediate retribution yet remains free from affliction or anger; he reaches the hells yet is devoid of all defilements and stains;
he reaches the animal realm yet is free from ignorance; he reaches the realm of hungry ghosts yet is fully endowed with meritorious conduct.

Within the paths of the form and formless realms, he does not regard them as superior; he manifests the practice of desire yet remains detached from all attachments; he manifests the practice of anger yet...
To all sentient beings who are without anger or obstruction, he manifests the practice of folly yet tames their minds with wisdom;
and so on, up to manifesting entry into false deliverance yet delivering all sentient beings through true deliverance;
and manifesting entry into the various paths while severing their causal conditions. The Commentary states: "The twelve causal conditions consist of three kinds of paths, namely: afflictions..."
All suffering arising from karma is not the Path; none escape these three categories. Why? Because the ten realms encompass all paths:
nine are not the Path, while only the Buddha-dharma realm is called the Buddha-path.

The six realms of existence consist of conditioned twelvefold dependent origination, whereas the Three Vehicles consist of unconditioned twelvefold dependent origination. To be unable to realize and penetrate this is bondage; all else is not liberation.

If one knows that within a single thought-moment of the Buddha-way, the principle of the twelve links of dependent origination encompasses the threefold path of the ten realms—that is the principle of the three seeds of the Tathāgata and the three types of Buddha-nature;
it is the principle of inconceivable wisdom, which is the non-path through which one penetrates the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, it is said: "To contemplate this mind produced by the causal conditions of the five heinous crimes as being emptiness, the provisional, and the middle."
The causes of the five heinous offenses within the stainless samādhi are themselves the path of afflictions and the path of karma—the non-path that leads to the three miserable realms.
This is the non-path of the path of suffering; yet even such most evil causes and effects can still lead to the penetration of the Buddha-way.
It is by this principle that those who are free from vexation and anger penetrate the fact that, fundamentally, there is no offense or evil, and thus they may commit what appears to be an offense.

This means that by receiving all sensations through non-reception, one teaches countless people so that they may emerge from the hells and even attain penetration into the realm of animals, becoming free from faults such as ignorance;
this is precisely the Samādhi of Non-retrogression and other such states.
The phenomena and their underlying principles are utterly distinct, as stated in the *Commentary on the "Inconceivable" Chapter*:

"There are two aspects of the inconceivable: first, clarifying the inconceivability of the three virtues; second, clarifying the inconceivability of the fundamental and the manifested [traces] in relation to the lands.
Regarding the first, there are three types: first, true nature (*dharmatā*); second, real wisdom (*prajñā*); and third, skillful means (*upāya*). As the Sūtra says:
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess a liberation called "Inconceivable.
If a Bodhisattva abides in this liberation, they are able to place Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed. That which is liberation is the true nature; that which abides herein is actual wisdom.
That one is able to place Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed is expedient means. These are the three virtues of liberation.
"Detachment" (*tuō*) means the severance of principle. Regarding the inconceivable nature of the fundamental and the trace, as well as their reliance upon lands, the Sūtra states:

"Vimalakīrti, by means of his supernatural powers, went to the east to the land of the Buddha Sumerudīparāja, which is thirty-six times the number of sands of the Ganges away, and borrowed thirty-two thousand lion thrones;
these thrones were eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in height. All [of this] is...

Entering the room, there is no obstruction whatsoever; even taking up the great trichiliocosm like a potter’s wheel and placing it in the right palm to cast it beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—[the Commentary] states:

"The preceding chapter on the empty room represents the land [of *dharmadhātu*], clarifying only the ultimate emptiness and stillness of *nirvāṇa-prabhāsvara*. This, however, is merely the fundamental ground of the *dharmakāya*, which cannot [be fully encompassed]."
The traces of the inconceivable have not yet been clarified by thought; now, by employing supernatural power, he brings forth seats to clarify these traces.
Abiding in both pure and impure lands, he manifests inconceivable deeds—such as gathering Mount Sumeru, the great ocean, earth, water, fire, and wind into a single country to show them to all people.
Such matters as these are manifested within the environment of dependent retribution, being inconceivable and unfathomable.
Regarding these marks:
in the "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation," this matter is particularly extraordinary;
within the sutra, Vimalakīrti, by means of his supernormal powers, reveals to the great assembly the realm above, forty [thousand worlds away].

If, within the context of illumination, one speaks of "non-duality," this means that while illuminating, there is simultaneous quiescence; it is also called "entering.
If one speaks of "duality" by simultaneously illuminating the two truths, this means that while quiescent, there is simultaneous illumination; it is also called "emerging.
Thus, duality and non-duality—entering and emerging—are both discussed in terms of awakening; for the practitioner who illuminates the Dharma, these are both duality and non-duality.
As for the "gate" (mēn) of this Dharma, it refers to penetrating without obstruction the principle of duality and non-duality; thus it is called a gate.

if it is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the consoling exhortations proceed from the single mind of the three contemplations—emptiness, conventionality, and the Middle—to subdue [them], thereby achieving the aforementioned "rebuking" of the bodhisattvas.

If one is about to establish the subsequent section, the emptiness contemplation of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*) serves as the basis for the "Chapter on Observing Sentient Beings," while the conventionality contemplation of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) serves as the basis for the Buddha-way.

Taking the "Chapter on the Original Perfection" as the Middle Way of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) for entering the Gate of Non-duality, and taking the "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation" as the basis for not adhering to the Tripitaka—this is the meaning of the practice of *mahāyāna*.

Furthermore, the reason the four teachings are clarified before entering the room is to subdue and rebuke ordinary beings who are attached to pleasure; however, within the sutra itself, consolation comes first and rebuke follows.

The Dharma-realm is interpenetrating;
I shall now cite the textual commentary of Master Qingliang. He states: "The Dharma-realm is the unified single True Reality that universally encompasses all phenomena;
it is simply this one mind. When the mind fuses with all phenomena, it constitutes the four kinds of Dharma-realms. This is the first point.
1. The *dharmadhātu* as the realm of differentiation (*bheda*) has the meaning of "division" (*avaccheda*), because each individual distinction possesses its own limits.

2. The *dharmadhātu* as the realm of principle (*li*) has the meaning of "nature" (*prakṛti*), because all inexhaustible phenomena share one and the same nature. 3. The *dharmadhātu* of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*shili wuai*) possesses both the meanings of nature and division;
here, nature and division are mutually unobstructed. 4. The *dharmadhātu* of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*) comprises all phenomena with their respective limits.
Each and every phenomenon is identical to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), interpenetrating one another in infinite layers. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"The nature of phenomena pervades all places—within all sentient beings and all lands; throughout the three periods of time, there is nothing left out, yet it has no form or characteristic that can be apprehended.
Therefore, principle is itself phenomena, such that perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential manifestation; phenomena are themselves principle...
By principle, the sequential arrangement does not obstruct perfect interfusion: every single atom and every single land contains all lands; every single atom-body contains all bodies.
Their breadth and narrowness, their excellence and inferiority, are inconceivable; their pure and impure locations are inexhaustible.
These are but a brief outline of the Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.

The *Ṣaḍhetuvibhāṣā* states: "The efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is that which does not obstruct another.

The associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*) refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) which, through having the same aspect (*ākāra*), the same object (*ālambana*), and being conjoined together, act like close friends or acquaintances accomplishing a task in concert. The common cause (*sabhāgahetu*)..."
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) assist one another and mutually support each other through their own seeds as causes:
past wholesome dharmas act as causes for present wholesome dharmas, and present wholesome dharmas act as causes for future wholesome dharmas;
unwholesome and neutral dharmas are likewise so. As for universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*), there are eleven universal [factors] within the spheres of the Truths of Suffering and Origination.
As for the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*), it refers to performing causes of good or evil and obtaining results of good or evil; this is called the sixth cause.

The four conditions (*pratyaya*) are as described above. The five causes are termed "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*). Mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) proceed in immediate succession and continue without interruption.

The sequence for naming the conditions is as follows: because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) arise by depending on objects, they are called the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Because all phenomena do not create obstacles when they arise, this is called the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Furthermore, the mind and mental factors arise from four conditions;

the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) arise from three conditions, excluding the object-condition. All other mental factors and dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) [arise from four conditions].

Formations (*saṃskāra*) and form (*rūpa*) arise from two conditions; excluding the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are inferior and thus none arise from only a single condition.
Mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*) arise from five causes; excluding the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mental states and mental factors arise from two conditions, namely: the associated condition (*samprayukta-pratyaya*) and the non-obstructing condition (*avighna*).

According to your interpretation, one bird represents the extremely low state of birth and death, while the other bird represents the extremely high state of nirvana;

thus, their ascent and descent would be utterly contradictory, and their simultaneous flight would not be manifested. Furthermore, even if two birds were both flying together, if one flew low and did not fly high, or if one flew high and did not fly low, their "simultaneous flight" would be unestablished.
Moreover, our own school cites the "Half and Full" teachings regarding a single dharma to demonstrate their simultaneous flight.

Regarding the two dharmas: if one takes both the impermanence of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the permanence of the Buddha-fruit as being "fulfilled" together, these two things are distinct and their natures differ like a pear and a mango;

As for those who "dual-traverse," they observe that within birth-and-death there is both the permanent and the impermanent, and they observe that within the Buddha-fruit there is likewise both the permanent and the impermanent; they take the permanence of both birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa* as [the fulfillment].

The seven [stages] should be expanded to nine;
the twelve abodes encompass all stages. Regarding the twelve abodes:
first is the abode of the lineage (*gotra-vihāra*), which refers to being naturally virtuous and possessing the seeds of all Buddha-dharmas.
Because one has abandoned coarse afflictions within the body, there are two [stages]: the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).

This refers to all practices possessed by a bodhisattva from the initial generation of the mind until the attainment of the pure ground of mind; these are called the stage of practice through understanding. Third is the stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
This refers to the planting of various roots of goodness, the production of bodhi, and the departure from the five fears; this is called the stage of joy. These three stages are subsumed [here].

The first, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), consists of the four abodes of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*): namely, being endowed with natural ethical discipline (*prakṛti-śīla*), the non-practice of unwholesome conduct, vast compassion, and the purification of the roots of virtue (*kuśala-mūla*).
This comprises the second, the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), which consists of the five abodes of higher mental intention (*adhicitta-vihāra*):
namely, applying fervent diligence toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) and not sparing one’s body or life because of hearing the true Dharma.

The third stage, the Luminous (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), comprises the six abodes of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā-vihāra*): namely, conventional pure knowledge, the samādhi of reality (*tattva-samādhi*), and the thorough observation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
This includes the fourth stage, the Radiant (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), which comprises the seven abodes associated with the truths (*satya-pratisaṃyukta-vihāra*):
namely, the observation of the truths through the factors conducive to enlightenment, the increase of merit, and the complete contemplation [of them].
The fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjaya*), is comprised of the eighth dwelling in accordance with the arising and ceasing of dependent origination;

this refers to the manifestation before one of unobstructed wisdom that is well able to discern the arising of suffering through causes and conditions, and the cessation of suffering through causes and conditions.
The sixth stage, the Manifest (*abhimukhī*), is comprised of the ninth dwelling in signlessness with practice and development; this refers to [the stage] based on the aforementioned six.
Because of the three kinds of wisdom in the seventh and eighth stages, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) is developed;

in every thought-moment, one becomes fully endowed with the ten *pāramitās* and all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*). This is not like other dwellings. Within this ninth dwelling, there are further eight dwellings:
first, the dwelling of joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*); second, the dwelling free from the stains of immoral conduct; third, the dwelling of increasing aspiration; fourth, the dwelling... [text continues].
Entering the Path at the fifth stage (*vihāra*), one engages in worldly activities at the sixth stage; this seventh stage enters the profound Dharma-gate.
From this, all Buddha-dharmas arise, and the auxiliary factors for enlightenment reach fulfillment as one sequentially enters the eighth stage, which is exclusively pure.
This comprises the seventh stage, the "Far-Reaching" (*dūraṃgamā*), characterized by the ten non-practices, non-development, and signlessness.
This subsumes the eleven bodhisattva dwellings of the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*); this [subsumes] the twelfth supreme dwelling of the Good Intelligence Ground (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*);
and this subsumes the Cloud of Dharma Ground (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
The seventh dwelling of the bodhisattva corresponds to the seventh Ground, the Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).
If one follows the forward progression, this corresponds to the seventh stage; if one follows the direct correspondence, it refers to the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjaya*).
To speak of it as corresponding to a "far traveler" refers to the seventh of the nine abodes characterized by effort and development.
